options: Fast ballistic movements performed with eyes closed to challenge inner vestibular receptors
Slow, precise, repetitive movements performed with visual guidance and high conscious focus
High-resistance maximal strength training performed on multi-joint gym weight machines
Passive stretching routines performed while resting supine on a physical therapy table
explanation: Frenkel exercises use slow, precise, repeated movements with visual guidance and conscious control. They are classically used for sensory ataxia and proprioceptive loss; they are not a universal treatment for every cerebellar disorder.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: On the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) for grading muscle spasticity, a score of '1+' is defined as:
options: No increase in tone or resistance during passive movement
A catch with minimal resistance through under half the remaining range
Considerable increase in tone that makes passive movement difficult
Marked increase in tone through most of the range but the part is easily moved
explanation: Modified Ashworth 1+ is a catch followed by minimal resistance through less than half of the remaining range. A catch-and-release at the end of range is Grade 1.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In PNF rhythmic stabilization training for trunk and spinal stability, what type of muscle contractions are elicited?
options: Rapid alternating isotonic concentric-eccentric contractions against high-velocity resistance
Alternating isometric contractions of agonist and antagonist muscle groups against resistance
Continuous passive stretching held at terminal physiological range of motion for 60 seconds
High-velocity low-amplitude thrust manipulations directed across facet joint capsules
explanation: Rhythmic stabilization utilizes alternating isometric contractions of opposing muscle groups against multidirectional manual perturbations to enhance dynamic joint stability and trunk co-contraction.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / Magee
text: In the Wainner clinical prediction rule for Cervical Radiculopathy, which combination of four positive findings provides a post-test probability exceeding 90%?
options: Neer, Hawkins, and Speed tests, with 3 positive findings
Lachman, pivot-shift, and anterior-drawer tests, with 3 positive findings
Ober, Thomas, and Trendelenburg tests, with 3 positive findings
Spurling, ULTT1, cervical distraction, and cervical rotation below 60°
explanation: The Wainner cluster contains four findings: Spurling, ULTT1, cervical distraction, and cervical rotation below 60° toward the symptomatic side.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: In Cyriax's orthopedic assessment framework, an 'Empty End-Feel' encountered during passive range of motion is indicative of:
options: Significant pain stopping movement before any mechanical tissue resistance is reached
Hard, abrupt unyielding sensation with bone-to-bone contact stopping joint movement
Soft, spongy yielding sensation caused by muscle approximation stopping joint movement
Firm, elastic sensation with slight give caused by joint capsule tension at end-range
explanation: An empty end-feel occurs when the patient stops examination due to severe, intolerable pain before any true anatomical or mechanical resistance is felt, indicating severe acute inflammatory pathology, fracture, or neoplasm.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty & Monalisa Pattnaik
text: What is the hallmark clinical feature of Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS Type I / Reflex Sympathetic Dystrophy) following a minor sports extremity injury?
options: Complete anesthesia and numbness over a discrete single dermatomal nerve root territory
Disproportionate continuous burning pain, allodynia, hyperalgesia, and autonomic swelling
Symmetrical ascending flaccid paralysis beginning in the distal lower extremity muscles
Sudden loss of proprioception and vibratory sensation with completely normal pinprick
explanation: CRPS Type I presents with severe pain disproportionate to the inciting event, allodynia (pain from non-noxious stimuli), swelling, skin color/temperature changes, and abnormal sweating in the absence of a distinct peripheral nerve lesion.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty & Monalisa Pattnaik
text: During dry-needling pistoning of a myofascial trigger point, which response may occur when the needle engages a taut band?
options: Structural lysis (tearing of myofascial taut band)
Permanent ablation (denervation of alpha motor neurons)
Local twitch response: brief involuntary contraction of the taut band
Systemic release (discharge of high-dose corticosteroids)
explanation: A local twitch response is a brief involuntary contraction that may occur during dry needling when the needle engages a taut band; its presence does not prove mechanical disruption or biochemical normalization.

topic: sports physiotherapy and acute injury management
subtopic: Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine / BJSM Consensus
text: In the management of an acute Grade I ankle sprain on the field, the modern 'PEACE & LOVE' protocol supersedes RICE by emphasizing:
options: PEACE & LOVE: protect, educate, then progressively load and exercise; avoid routine anti-inflammatories
RICE protocol: absolute Rest, aggressive Ice, continuous Compression, and Elevation exclusively
PRICE protocol: Protection, complete Rest for 4 weeks, Ice every hour, Compression, Elevation
MEAT protocol: Movement, high-dose Exercise, aggressive Analgesics, and immediate Total loading
explanation: PEACE & LOVE expands to Protect, Elevate, Avoid routine anti-inflammatory modalities, Compress, Educate, followed by Load, Optimism, Vascularisation, and Exercise. It does not require avoiding every anti-inflammatory treatment in every clinical situation.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: When assessing joint range of motion, what is the standardized universal goniometer alignment for measuring active shoulder abduction?
options: Fulcrum at acromion; stationary arm parallel to trunk; moving arm along humerus to lateral epicondyle
Fulcrum at the medial epicondyle; stationary arm along the femur; moving arm along the tibia
Fulcrum at the patella; stationary arm along the pelvis; moving arm along the tibia
Fulcrum at the fibular head; stationary arm along the femur; moving arm toward the calcaneus
explanation: For shoulder abduction, align the fulcrum with the lateral acromion, the stationary arm with the trunk/sternum, and the moving arm with the lateral humerus.

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: In shoulder instability, a 'Bankart Lesion' refers to an avulsion tear of which specific anatomical structure?
options: Anteroinferior glenoid labrum avulsion detachment, often with anterior capsular stretching
Superior glenoid labrum tear extending anteriorly and posteriorly at biceps tendon anchor
Impaction compression fracture of the posterolateral humeral head against anterior rim
Complete avulsion of the supraspinatus tendon from the greater tubercle of the humerus
explanation: A Bankart lesion is a detachment of the anterior-inferior glenoid labrum from the glenoid rim resulting from anterior shoulder dislocation, compromising anterior glenohumeral stability.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: Which test evaluates scapular contribution by manually stabilizing or retracting the medial scapular border during an active shoulder test?
options: Scapular Retraction Test, using scapular stabilization during testing
Scapular Depression Test, using downward scapular stabilization
Scapular Tilt Test, using posterior scapular tilting
Scapular Assistance Test, assisting upward rotation and posterior tilt
explanation: Stabilizing or retracting the medial scapular border describes the Scapular Retraction Test. The Scapular Assistance Test instead assists upward rotation and posterior tilt during elevation.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The Dial Test (Tibial External Rotation test) is performed at 30° and 90° of knee flexion. Increased external rotation >10° at 30° flexion that decreases at 90° indicates isolated injury to which structure?
options: Isolated posterolateral-corner injury
ACL injury diagnosed by Lachman testing
Meniscal injury diagnosed by McMurray testing
PCL injury diagnosed by posterior drawer testing
explanation: Increased external rotation at 30° that normalizes at 90° suggests an isolated posterolateral-corner injury; increased rotation at both angles suggests combined PLC and PCL injury.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: When performing the Slump Test for neural tension, what is the standard proximal-to-distal sequence of positioning?
options: Slump spine, flex neck, extend knee, dorsiflex ankle, then release neck
Perform Apley compression prone with knee flexion and tibial rotation
Perform Thessaly standing with partial knee flexion and trunk rotation
Perform McMurray supine with knee flexion and tibial rotation
explanation: The slump sequence progressively loads the neural tissues and then uses cervical release as structural differentiation.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The Crank Test for shoulder labral pathology is performed in supine by placing the glenohumeral joint in which position while applying axial load?
options: Approximately 160° scapular-plane elevation with axial compression and humeral rotation
90° elevation with forced internal rotation, no axial compression, and no humeral rotation
90° abduction in an empty-can position without axial compression or humeral rotation
90° forward flexion with forearm supination and no axial compression or humeral rotation
explanation: The Crank test uses high scapular-plane elevation, axial compression, and humeral rotation to stress the glenoid labrum.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The Mulders Sign test is performed on the foot by squeezing the metatarsal heads together while palpating the intermetatarsal space to diagnose:
options: Tarsal tunnel syndrome with posterior tibial nerve entrapment
Morton's Neuroma with interdigital nerve click on compression
Stress fracture of second metatarsal shaft with bone edema
Plantar fasciitis at calcaneal insertion with morning pain
explanation: Mulder's click is elicited by compressing the metatarsal heads transversally while applying plantar/dorsal pressure in the intermetatarsal space; a palpable click and sharp radiating pain confirm Morton's neuroma.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The Hornblower's Sign (Patte Test) evaluates the functional structural integrity of which external rotator cuff muscle?
options: Teres minor
Infraspinatus
Supraspinatus
Subscapularis
explanation: Hornblower’s sign assesses the ability to maintain external rotation at 90° abduction and is associated particularly with teres-minor dysfunction or a large posterosuperior cuff tear.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The Belly-Press (Napoleon) test and Lift-Off test are clinical diagnostic tests used specifically to assess:
options: Serratus anterior winging during active forward arm elevation against a wall
Subscapularis integrity and internal rotation strength on abdominal press
Long head of biceps instability in groove during resisted elbow flexion drills
Infraspinatus tendon tear at greater tuberosity with external rotation lag
explanation: The Lift-Off test (hand behind back) and Belly-Press test (pressing palm into abdomen with wrist straight) specifically evaluate the subscapularis muscle and tendon integrity.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The Ely's Test is performed with the patient in prone position to evaluate contracture or tightness of which muscle?
options: Rectus Femoris: knee flexion produces anterior pelvic tilt
Biceps femoris: knee flexion produces posterior pelvic tilt
Iliopsoas muscle: knee flexion produces lateral pelvic tilt
Gluteus maximus: knee flexion produces neutral pelvic balance
explanation: Ely's test passively flexes the knee in prone; if the ipsilateral hip flexes and the pelvis rises off the table, it indicates tightness/shortening of the two-joint Rectus Femoris.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The Noble Compression Test for Iliotibial Band Friction Syndrome produces pain over the lateral femoral epicondyle as the knee is passively moved from 90° flexion through what specific angle?
options: 0 to 5 degrees of knee hyperextension during terminal locking on couch
120 to 140 degrees of deep knee flexion on examination couch in clinic
60 to 75 degrees of knee flexion during mid-range loading on couch
25 to 30 degrees of knee flexion during epicondyle compression test
explanation: Noble's test compresses the ITB over the lateral femoral epicondyle while extending the knee; pain peaks at ~30° flexion where the posterior fibers of the ITB slide anteriorly over the epicondyle.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby
text: In therapeutic exercise progression, what is the 'SAID Principle'?
options: Sustained Aerobic Intensity Decreases across weekly training cycles
Specific Adaptations to Imposed Demands as body adapts to applied load
Skeletal Articulations Immobilize following unaccustomed training bouts
Strength And Intensity Diminish during competition taper phases
explanation: The SAID principle (Specific Adaptations to Imposed Demands) dictates that the body will adapt specifically to the exact physiological, biomechanical, and metabolic stress imposed during training.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby
text: In the rehabilitation of shoulder impingement, which exercise elicits high electromyographic (EMG) activity in the Lower Trapezius while minimizing Upper Trapezius dominance?
options: Prone Y-raise in the scapular plane and prone horizontal abduction in external rotation
Heavy shoulder shrugs with dumbbells in standing position to complete fatigue
Upright barbell rows pulled directly to chin level with narrow hand grip width
Overhead military barbell press performed to failure on a gym exercise bench
explanation: EMG studies (Cools et al.) demonstrate that prone Y-raises (at 120° scaption with thumbs up) and prone horizontal abduction in external rotation maximize lower trapezius recruitment while minimizing upper trapezius co-activation.

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: In closed kinetic chain squatting, why does increasing trunk forward lean (hip flexion) reduce patellofemoral joint stress while increasing hip extensor demand?
options: It shifts body weight onto gastrocnemius, reducing quadriceps demand in squat
It moves ground reaction force closer to knee and further from hip in squat
It unloads gluteus maximus and hamstrings during downward descent in squat
It forces the patella to translate laterally in trochlear groove during squat
explanation: Forward trunk lean changes the ground-reaction-force moment arms: it tends to reduce the knee-extensor moment while increasing the hip-extensor moment, increasing demand on the gluteal and hamstring musculature.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby
text: According to Kaltenborn's manual therapy grading system, a Grade III Traction mobilization is defined as:
options: A high-velocity thrust manipulation performed at end of passive range
Applying sustained linear traction beyond slack to stretch joint capsule
A small-amplitude movement that neutralizes joint pressure in capsule
Taking up joint slack and tightening surrounding tissues in capsule
explanation: Kaltenborn Grade III traction applies sufficient force to take up joint slack and stretch periarticular soft tissues to increase mobility and restore joint play.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise - Kisner & Colby / Brukner & Khan
text: In the rehabilitation of an acute inversion ankle sprain, which muscle group requires priority concentric and eccentric strengthening to resist dynamic inversion forces?
options: Peroneus Longus and Brevis evertors along lateral lower leg compartment
Gastrocnemius and Soleus deep plantarflexors on posterior calcaneus bone
Tibialis anterior and Extensor hallucis along anterior shank compartment
Tibialis posterior and Flexor digitorum in deep posterior calf compartment
explanation: The peroneus longus and brevis are the primary dynamic lateral stabilizers of the ankle; their rapid eccentric contraction counteracts sudden forced inversion, protecting the ATFL and CFL.

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: During open-chain knee rehabilitation, why is isotonic knee extension from 90° to 45° of flexion considered safe for the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL)?
options: The patella locks the joint at 45 degrees, eliminating anterior shear forces
Quadriceps contraction cannot generate extensor torque at 90 degrees flexion
Hamstring muscles are completely inhibited at 90 degrees of seated flexion
In 90° to 45° flexion, anterior tibial shear and ACL tensile strain are minimal
explanation: Open-chain knee extension from 90° toward 45° generally produces less anterior tibial shear and less ACL strain than terminal extension. The strain is reduced, not literally zero.

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Neumann / Brukner & Khan
text: What is the established biomechanical role of the lower extremities and trunk during an overhead throw?
options: They contribute little, while the arm generates nearly all throwing force
They contribute only after ball release, during the final hand motion
They contribute substantially through the proximal-to-distal kinetic chain
They contribute only by flexing the wrist at release, not by driving the throw
explanation: The lower extremities and trunk contribute substantially through a proximal-to-distal kinetic chain. A universal percentage is not established across all throwing sports and athletes.

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: In foot and ankle biomechanics, the 'Windlass Mechanism' is engaged during terminal stance and toe-off when:
options: The calcaneus slides laterally away from cuboid, flattening longitudinal arch
The Achilles tendon relaxes to allow maximum flat-foot pronation in midfoot
The first MTP joint extends, tightening plantar fascia and elevating medial arch
The ankle is forcefully inverted while toes flex into the floor during stance
explanation: The Windlass mechanism (Hicks) occurs during terminal stance toe-off when 1st MTP extension pulls the plantar fascia tight around the metatarsal heads, elevating the medial arch and transforming the foot into a rigid lever for propulsion.

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: Which foot posture during running increases tensile stress on the plantar fascia and posterior tibial tendon?
options: Pes cavus with rigid high arch and supination during loading response phase
Neutral foot alignment with symmetrical rearfoot motion throughout stance phase
Pes planus with excessive prolonged subtalar pronation and midfoot eversion
Walking exclusively on lateral 5th metatarsal border in continuous inversion
explanation: Excessive or prolonged pronation lowers the medial longitudinal arch, stretching the plantar fascia and overworking the Tibialis Posterior as it eccentrically attempts to decelerate internal tibial rotation and arch collapse.

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: In hip biomechanics, why does holding a walking cane in the hand CONTRALATERAL to an injured or osteoarthritic hip significantly reduce joint reaction forces?
options: It creates a supportive torque assisting abductors, reducing joint contact load
It locks the injured hip into 90 degrees internal rotation during stance phase
It triples the ground reaction force transferred onto ipsilateral knee joint
It forces the patient to hop purely on contralateral healthy limb during gait
explanation: A contralateral cane provides a long moment arm to the pelvis; pressing down creates a moment that opposes pelvic drop, drastically reducing the required contraction force of the ipsilateral gluteus medius and lowering hip joint reaction force by ~50%.

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: What is the primary function of the Menisci of the knee joint during axial weight-bearing?
options: Transmitting 50% to 70% of compressive loads and providing secondary stability
Eliminating 100% of all friction and shear forces between femur and tibia
Locking the knee joint into rigid full extension during the 60% swing phase
Producing active extensor torque equal to 100% of quadriceps contraction
explanation: The menisci convert axial compressive loads into hoop stresses, transmitting ~50–70% of compressive force, doubling joint contact area, and reducing peak stress on articular cartilage.

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: In scapular kinematics, 'scapular winging' characterized by prominence of the entire medial border and inferior angle of the scapula is caused by paralysis or weakness of:
options: Serratus Anterior muscle (Long Thoracic Nerve root C5–C7)
Latissimus Dorsi muscle (Thoracodorsal Nerve root C6–C8)
Rhomboid Major muscle (Dorsal Scapular Nerve root C4–C5)
Trapezius muscle (Spinal Accessory Cranial Nerve C1–C5)
explanation: Weakness or long thoracic nerve palsy of the Serratus Anterior causes classic medial scapular winging (medial border and inferior angle lifting away from posterior ribcage, especially during push-ups or arm elevation).

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: Compared with the lumbar spine, which region permits more axial rotation because of its relatively coronal facet orientation?
options: Thoracic spine (T1 to T12 segments with coronal facet joint orientation)
Lumbar spine (L1 to L5 segments with sagittal facet joint orientation)
Cervical spine (C1 to C7 segments with 45-degree facet joint orientation)
Sacral spine (S1 to S5 fused segments with zero intersegmental motion)
explanation: Thoracic facet joints are oriented in the frontal (coronal) plane, facilitating axial rotation while restricting flexion/extension; lumbar facets are in the sagittal plane, blocking rotation.

subtopic: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Perry & Burnfield
text: In normal human gait, what is the primary role of the Quadriceps muscle group during the Loading Response phase?
options: Eccentric contraction to absorb impact shock and control knee flexion
Concentric contraction to accelerate the knee into terminal extension
Isometric contraction to lock the tibiofemoral joint in extension
Passive relaxation allowing ground reaction forces to stabilize knee
explanation: At loading response, the quadriceps contract eccentrically to yield to the external knee flexion moment, absorbing ground impact shock while limiting knee flexion to ~15°.

subtopic: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Perry & Burnfield
text: A 'Vaulting Gait' is a pathological compensation where the patient rises up on the toes of the stance limb. Why is this compensation used?
options: To increase propulsion power of ipsilateral stance limb during push-off phase
To assist toe clearance of a longer or non-flexing contralateral swing limb
To compensate for severe quadriceps spasticity in ipsilateral stance knee
To reduce compressive ground reaction impact forces across lumbar spine
explanation: Vaulting involves premature plantarflexion on the sound stance limb to elevate the pelvis, creating extra ground clearance for a contralateral swing limb that cannot functionally shorten (due to knee stiffness, cast, or foot drop).

subtopic: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Perry & Burnfield
text: In running gait biomechanics, what is the key kinematic distinction that differentiates running from walking?
options: Running has a longer double-support stance phase than quiet walking
Running completely eliminates all vertical ground reaction forces
Running requires zero active hamstring or quadriceps participation
Running involves a flight phase and lacks a double-support phase
explanation: Walking is characterized by periods of double limb support (both feet on ground); running eliminates double support and introduces a flight (float) phase where neither foot contacts the ground.

subtopic: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Perry & Burnfield
text: In running ground reaction force analysis, a 'Rearfoot Strike' (heel strike) pattern is characterized on force-time curves by:
options: A smooth dome-shaped force curve without any initial transient peak
A linear ramp curve reaching peak ground reaction force at push-off
A prominent, sharp initial impact transient peak occurring early on
A flat horizontal line maintaining constant force throughout stance
explanation: A rearfoot strike exhibits a distinct impact transient peak (vertical impact force spike occurring in the first 15–30 ms), whereas a forefoot/midfoot strike typically smooths out or eliminates this impact peak.

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson
text: Which statement best reflects the use of polarity in HVPC for acute oedema and wound care?
options: Positive polarity is mandatory in every acute oedema protocol and wound treatment
Negative polarity is common early; selection depends on healing phase and protocol
Alternating current has no polarity and is required for every acute wound
Direct current is used to cauterize the skin during wound care
explanation: HVPC polarity is protocol- and healing-phase-dependent. Cathodal/negative treatment is commonly used in some early oedema and wound protocols, while later wound-healing goals may use different polarity choices.

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson
text: In therapeutic ultrasound, the 'Effective Radiating Area' (ERA) of the transducer crystal is clinically defined as:
options: The crystal area that emits ultrasonic energy (effective area)
The total surface area of the soundhead housing (geometric area)
The spatial depth to which acoustic waves penetrate (depth area)
The ratio of peak intensity to average intensity (intensity area)
explanation: The ERA is the cross-sectional area of the ultrasound beam exiting the treatment head, determined by the vibrating piezoelectric crystal, and is always slightly smaller than the total geometric faceplate area.

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson
text: What is the Beam Non-uniformity Ratio (BNR) in therapeutic ultrasound, and what is the clinically acceptable standard ratio?
options: The ratio of crystal surface area to soundhead geometric housing area, not beam intensity
Spatial peak intensity divided by spatial average intensity; acceptable BNR is no more than six-to-one
The ratio of acoustic oscillation frequency to electrical power delivered by the transducer
The ratio of half-value-layer absorption depth to wave velocity in the treated tissue
explanation: BNR is the ratio of spatial peak intensity to spatial average intensity. A typical acceptable BNR is no more than 6:1; lower values indicate a more uniform beam and less hot-spot risk.

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson
text: When applying therapeutic ultrasound at a frequency of 3 MHz compared to 1 MHz, how does the depth of tissue penetration differ?
options: 3 MHz penetrates deeply; 1 MHz is absorbed superficially in skin
3 MHz is absorbed superficially; 1 MHz penetrates deeply in muscle
Both 1 MHz and 3 MHz penetrate to identical physiological depths
Neither 1 MHz nor 3 MHz can penetrate through cutaneous layers
explanation: Higher frequency (3 MHz) is absorbed more rapidly and penetrates superficially (1–2.5 cm, ideal for superficial tendons), while lower frequency (1 MHz) attenuates slower and reaches deep structures (3–5 cm, ideal for deep muscle/capsule).

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In proprioceptive neurorehabilitation, what is the primary function of the Golgi Tendon Organ (GTO)?
options: Monitoring muscle length changes and mediating reciprocal inhibition of others
Monitoring muscle tension and force, mediating autogenic inhibition in tendon
Detecting joint position acceleration and stimulating alpha motor neuron drive
Inhibiting all voluntary corticospinal motor unit recruitment in active limbs
explanation: GTOs are encapsulated receptors located in series at the musculotendinous junction that monitor active muscle tension and exert autogenic inhibition (Ib afferents) on the agonist motor neuron pool to prevent excessive overload.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In the assessment of balance and vestibular function, the Sensory Organization Test (SOT / Dynamic Posturography) systematically isolates which three sensory systems?
options: Visual, Somatosensory (proprioceptive), and Vestibular systems
Auditory, Olfactory (chemoreceptive), and Gustatory brain systems
Cardiovascular, Respiratory (pulmonary), and Endocrine systems
Sympathetic, Parasympathetic (vagal), and Enteric gut systems
explanation: The SOT evaluates balance under 6 conditions by systematically disrupting visual and somatosensory inputs to determine how effectively the central nervous system integrates visual, proprioceptive, and vestibular inputs.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In spinal cord injury rehabilitation, an athlete presenting with 'Brown-Séquard Syndrome' (hemisection of the spinal cord) will demonstrate:
options: Bilateral loss of all motor and sensory function below the level of lesion
Ipsilateral loss of motor/proprioception; contralateral loss of pain/temp
Contralateral loss of motor function; ipsilateral loss of touch sensation
Isolated loss of deep tendon reflexes without any sensory or motor changes
explanation: Hemisection of the cord damages uncrossed corticospinal tracts and dorsal columns (causing ipsilateral motor and proprioceptive loss) and crossed spinothalamic tracts (causing contralateral pain/temperature loss).

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In upper motor neuron lesions, what is the 'Clasp-Knife Response' observed during rapid passive stretching of a spastic muscle?
options: Continuous lead-pipe resistance to passive stretch across the entire range
Cogwheel ratcheting resistance during passive movement throughout available range
Marked initial resistance followed by abrupt giving-way of resistance to stretch
Flaccid zero resistance to passive movement across all physiological motions
explanation: The clasp-knife phenomenon is a hallmark of spasticity where rapid passive stretch encounters high initial resistance (stretch reflex hyper-excitability) followed by sudden melting/giving-way of tone.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / Cyriax
text: In Cyriax's selective tissue tension testing, a finding of 'Painful and Strong' on resisted isometric testing indicates:
options: A major structural rupture of tendon or bone with gross weakness
A minor structural lesion of muscle or tendon with localized pain
A severe neurological nerve root avulsion lesion with numbness
Normal healthy physiological connective tissue without injury
explanation: Cyriax classification: (1) Strong & Pain-free = Normal; (2) Strong & Painful = Minor lesion/tendinitis/grade I strain; (3) Weak & Painful = Major lesion/fracture; (4) Weak & Pain-free = Complete rupture or neurological deficit.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / Cyriax
text: In Cyriax's selective tissue tension testing, a finding of 'Weak and Pain-Free' on resisted isometric testing classically indicates:
options: Complete structural rupture of tendon/muscle or a severe neurological nerve lesion
A minor structural strain or low-grade tendinopathy of contracting muscle unit
Severe joint capsular adhesions and extensive intra-articular capsular fibrosis
Psychogenic non-organic pain amplification without structural tissue injury
explanation: Weak and Pain-Free indicates that the muscle cannot generate force but does not hurt during contraction, characteristic of complete tendon tear (no tension on fibers) or neurological denervation.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: What is the primary diagnostic indicator of 'Thoracic Outlet Syndrome' (TOS) during the Roos Elevated Arm Stress Test (EAST)?
options: Distal paresthesia, ischemic discomfort, or inability to keep the arms elevated
Pain-free hand opening and closing with no symptoms for the full test duration
Isolated low-back pain during a straight-leg raise without arm symptoms
Localized acromioclavicular clicking without arm fatigue or paresthesia
explanation: In Roos EAST, the patient holds arms at 90° abduction/ER and slowly opens/closes hands for 3 minutes; reproduction of ischemic pain, distal paresthesias, or inability to hold arms up indicates neurovascular TOS.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: During Adson's Test for vascular Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, what clinical change in the radial pulse constitutes a positive test?
options: Diminution or loss of radial pulse with head turned to tested side and neck extended
Increase in radial pulse volume with head turned away from the tested upper limb
Sudden drop in blood pressure when raising the arms overhead in standing position
Reproduction of sharp pain along the lateral epicondyle during resisted wrist flexion
explanation: Adson's test compresses the subclavian artery between the anterior and middle scalene muscles; diminution or loss of the radial pulse with deep inspiration and ipsilateral neck rotation/extension indicates scalene entrapment.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby
text: In orthopedic manual therapy, what is the 'Treatment Plane' as defined by Kaltenborn?
options: A plane lying in concave articular surface, parallel to surface and perpendicular to axis
A plane lying strictly in the convex articular surface, parallel to long bone shaft
A vertical anatomical plane dividing the human body into symmetrical right and left halves
A horizontal transverse plane dividing the joint cavity into equal upper and lower halves
explanation: Kaltenborn defines the treatment plane as lying on the concave articular surface. Traction is applied perpendicular to this plane, while joint gliding is applied parallel to it.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / Magee
text: When assessing sacroiliac joint dysfunction, which clinical test cluster (Laslett Cluster) provides the highest diagnostic accuracy when at least 2 of 4 tests are positive?
options: Distraction Test, Compression Test, Thigh Thrust Test, and Sacral Thrust Test
Lachman Test, Anterior Drawer Test, Pivot Shift Test, and Godfrey Sag Test
Neer Test, Hawkins Test, Empty Can Test, and Speed Test across shoulder joint
Ober Test, Thomas Test, Ely Test, and Trendelenburg Test across the hip joint
explanation: A positive Laslett provocation cluster supports the SI joint as a possible pain source with useful diagnostic accuracy; it does not confirm a structural SI-joint lesion or establish a single pathology without clinical correlation.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In the management of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) affecting the posterior semicircular canal, which particle repositioning maneuver is the gold standard therapy?
options: Brandt-Daroff habituation exercises performed twice daily at home
Semont liberatory maneuver performed into contralateral side-lying
Epley Maneuver canalith repositioning for posterior canal BPPV
Passive cervical traction delivered on a motorized traction couch
explanation: The Epley maneuver systematically rotates the head through 4 positions to move free-floating otoconia (canaliths) out of the posterior semicircular canal back into the utricle, resolving BPPV with high efficacy.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The Thessaly Test for meniscal tear assessment demonstrates its highest diagnostic accuracy when performed at what joint angle and functional condition?
options: Standing single-leg weight bearing with knee flexed to 20° and rotating
Prone passive knee flexion to 90° with applied axial joint compression
Supine passive hip and knee flexion to 90° with dynamic tibial rotation
Seated active knee extension from 90° to 0° against manual resistance
explanation: Karachalios et al. demonstrated that the Thessaly test at 20° knee flexion with dynamic weight-bearing rotation loads the menisci dynamically, achieving diagnostic accuracy >90% for meniscal pathology.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The 'External Rotation Lag Sign' (Infraspinatus Spring-back test) is performed with the shoulder at 90° abduction and near-maximal external rotation. Inability to maintain this position indicates tear of:
options: Subscapularis muscle tendon belly along the anterior scapular fossa
Infraspinatus and/or Supraspinatus tendon complex at greater tuberosity
Teres Major muscle tendon inserting into the medial bicipital groove
Pectoralis Major tendon inserting into the lateral lip of bicipital groove
explanation: The External Rotation Lag Sign (Hertel) evaluates infraspinatus/supraspinatus integrity; if the patient's arm lags/springs forward internally, it confirms significant structural rotator cuff tear.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The 'Drop-Arm Test' (Codman's Sign) is positive when an athlete cannot smoothly control lowering the arm from 90° abduction, indicating full-thickness tear of:
options: Biceps Brachii long head tendon in the intertubercular bicipital groove
Infraspinatus muscle tendon belly along the infraspinous scapular fossa
Supraspinatus tendon with arm suddenly dropping to side with severe pain
Subscapularis muscle tendon inserting into the lesser humeral tuberosity
explanation: In Codman's Drop-Arm test, passive abduction to 90° is released; if the patient cannot slowly lower the arm eccentrically and it drops abruptly, a full-thickness supraspinatus tear is present.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee / Bennell et al.
text: The 'Knee-to-Wall Test' (Weight-Bearing Lunge Test - WBLT) provides an objective clinical measure of:
options: Weight-bearing ankle dorsiflexion range of motion measured on floor
Non-weight-bearing ankle plantarflexion strength measured on chair
Subtalar joint inversion and eversion total angular range of motion
First metatarsophalangeal joint extension mobility in quiet standing
explanation: The WBLT measures closed-chain ankle dorsiflexion mobility (distance from big toe to wall with heel kept down); values <9–10 cm indicate restricted dorsiflexion and heightened lower limb injury risk.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The Stork Standing Test may reproduce pain in athletes with which suspected spine condition?
options: Lumbar Spondylolysis / Pars stress fracture on weight-bearing side
Thoracic structural scoliosis with severe rib cage deformity in spine
Coccygodynia and coccygeal subluxation following a direct trauma fall
Acute cervical disc herniation with severe spinal cord compression
explanation: The one-legged hyperextension test may reproduce pain in athletes with suspected pars stress injury, but its diagnostic accuracy is limited and it should not independently diagnose spondylolysis.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The 'Phalen's Test' is performed for 60 seconds by holding the wrists in maximal unforced flexion. What constitutes a positive finding indicative of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome?
options: Paresthesia in the ulnar nerve distribution (little finger and half ring)
Paresthesia in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle finger)
Numbness over the lateral shoulder deltoid patch (axillary nerve territory)
Burning pain over the anatomical snuffbox (superficial radial nerve)
explanation: Phalen's test increases carpal tunnel pressure; numbness/tingling in the median nerve sensory distribution within 60 seconds indicates median nerve compression in the carpal canal.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The 'Froment's Sign' evaluates ulnar nerve motor function. When the patient attempts to pinch a piece of paper between the thumb and index finger against resistance, a positive test is manifested by:
options: Hyper-extension of thumb MCP joint by Extensor Pollicis Longus tendon
Weakness of index-finger flexion caused by isolated median-nerve injury
Compensatory flexion of thumb IP joint by FPL due to Adductor palsy
Spontaneous violent abduction of all fingers away from the paper grip
explanation: Froment's sign tests the ulnar-innervated Adductor Pollicis; weakness causes the patient to substitute by forcefully flexing the thumb IP joint using the median-innervated Flexor Pollicis Longus.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The 'Apprehension Test' for Anterior Shoulder Instability is performed with the patient supine and the shoulder in 90° abduction and maximal external rotation. What is considered a true positive test?
options: 90° Shoulder Flexion with 90° Internal Rotation on couch
Apprehension or fear with resistance to further external rotation
0° Shoulder Extension with 90° Forearm Pronation on couch
0° Neutral Adduction with 90° Internal Rotation on couch
explanation: True positive apprehension is marked by athlete alarm and resistance to further motion due to fear of anterior subluxation/dislocation (relieved by the Jobe Relocation test where posterior force is applied).

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby / Khan
text: In the 'Optimal Loading' paradigm (POLICE / PEACE & LOVE), why is progressive mechanical loading superior to prolonged complete immobilization in soft tissue injuries?
options: Prolonged immobilization doubles skeletal muscle glycogen content in limbs
Mechanical loading prevents white blood cells from entering healing beds
Mechanical loading stimulates mechanotransduction and collagen alignment
Immobilization leads to permanent bony ankylosis across all human joints
explanation: Mechanotransduction converts physiological mechanical loading into cellular biochemical signals (upregulating tenocyte/fibroblast collagen I synthesis), optimizing scar alignment and tissue tensile strength.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise - Kisner & Colby / Brukner & Khan
text: In knee rehabilitation, what is the 'Envelope of Function' concept described by Scott Dye?
options: The surgical fibrous capsule enclosing intra-articular synovial fluid
The total number of exercise repetitions performed in a single workout
The range of physiological load a joint can withstand without injury
The psychological mental boundary preventing athlete competition fear
explanation: Scott Dye's 'Envelope of Function' defines the dynamic boundary of load and frequency that a joint/tissue can sustain while maintaining structural and metabolic homeostasis (loading beyond causes pain/degeneration).

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise - Kisner & Colby / Neumann
text: In eccentric resistance exercise, why does high-load eccentric training elicit greater muscle damage (microtrauma) and mechanical tension than concentric training?
options: Eccentric exercise completely blocks calcium release from ryanodine gates
Fewer motor units handle high loads, causing higher strain per sarcomere
Eccentric contractions produce zero ATP and cause chemical tissue necrosis
Concentric contractions generate three times higher mechanical tendon forces
explanation: Eccentric muscle contractions recruit fewer motor units for a given load, concentrating immense force across a smaller cross-sectional area of active fibers, leading to sarcomere overstretch ('popping sarcomere theory') and robust remodeling stimuli.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby
text: In the Maitland concept, what is the clinical distinction between a joint 'Stiffness' dominant problem versus a 'Pain' dominant problem?
options: There is zero clinical distinction between pain and stiffness problems
Stiffness conditions receive exclusively superficial cold packs on couch
Pain conditions require immediate high-velocity Grade V joint thrusts
Pain-dominant gets Grade I–II oscillations; Stiffness gets Grade III–IV
explanation: In a pain-dominant problem, pain is encountered before the first resistance (P1 before R1), so lower-grade oscillations are generally selected. In a stiffness-dominant problem, resistance precedes pain and higher-grade oscillations may be used toward the restriction when appropriate.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby / McGill
text: In spinal rehabilitation, McGill's 'Big Three' core stabilization exercises designed to optimize spinal stability with minimal compressive loading are:
options: Standing good-mornings, standing heavy side bends, and Jefferson deadlifts
Modified Curl-up, Side Bridge plank, and Bird-Dog quadruped exercise
Seated Roman chair back extensions, heavy weighted sit-ups, Russian twists
Barbell overhead squats, hanging leg raises, and deep decline crunches
explanation: Stuart McGill's 'Big 3' (Modified Curl-Up, Side Bridge, and Bird-Dog) provide optimal 3D muscular endurance and motor control across the core with minimal spinal compressive and shear penalties.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise - Kisner & Colby / Brukner & Khan
text: In the management of Achilles tendinopathy, which exercise protocol incorporates concentric-eccentric calf raises with heavy backpacks or barbell loads performed 3 times per week?
options: Heavy Slow Resistance protocol with 6–15 RM loads and 6-second cadence
High-velocity open chain leg extensions performed with 6–15 RM loads
Passive complete immobilization in a cylinder cast for 6–15 weeks rest
High-dose corticosteroid injections directly into tendon for 6–15 days
explanation: For Achilles tendinopathy, Achilles-specific HSR protocols use progressive calf raises with heavy loads, commonly three times per week and a controlled concentric/eccentric tempo. Kongsgaard et al. is chiefly associated with the patellar-tendinopathy HSR trial, so the attribution should not be used for this Achilles-specific statement.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby
text: In PNF stretching, what is the recommended minimum duration for holding the isometric contraction phase in the 'Contract-Relax' technique?
options: 5 to 10 seconds of submaximal or maximal isometric hold to discharge GTOs
60 to 70 seconds of agonizing maximal strain to fatigue muscle fibers
0 to 1 seconds of hold as duration has zero influence on GTO activation
15 to 20 seconds of rapid pulsing contraction before stretch release
explanation: Holding the isometric contraction for 5–10 seconds adequately discharges Golgi Tendon Organ Ib afferents, initiating autogenic inhibition to allow greater muscle relaxation during the subsequent passive stretch.

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: In lower extremity biomechanics, during the closed-chain 'Subtalar Joint Pronation' that occurs during weight acceptance, what triplanar kinematic motions occur at the calcaneus and talus?
options: Calcaneal inversion, with talar abduction and talar dorsiflexion in stance
Complete superior displacement of cuboid bone away from calcaneal facet
Calcaneal eversion, with talar adduction and talar plantarflexion in stance
Calcaneal pure sagittal extension with zero horizontal or frontal rotation
explanation: Closed-chain subtalar pronation consists of calcaneal eversion (frontal plane), combined with talar adduction/medial rotation (transverse plane) and talar plantarflexion (sagittal plane), unlocking the midtarsal joint for shock absorption.

subtopic: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Jacquelin Perry & Judith M. Burnfield
text: During normal human gait, what is the total range of sagittal plane ankle motion required for normal function?
options: Approximately 10° of dorsiflexion and 20° of plantarflexion (total ~30°)
Approximately 30° of dorsiflexion and 45° of plantarflexion (total ~75°)
Approximately 0° of dorsiflexion and 5° of plantarflexion (total ~5°)
Approximately 45° of dorsiflexion and 60° of plantarflexion (total ~105°)
explanation: Normal walking gait requires ~10° of ankle dorsiflexion (achieved during late terminal stance) and ~20° of plantarflexion (achieved at push-off/toe-off), providing a total functional arc of ~30°.

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: In scapular kinematics, what is the primary plane and direction of motion produced by the Serratus Anterior muscle on the scapula?
options: Scapular protraction, upward rotation, and posterior tilting on thoracic cage
Scapular retraction, downward rotation, and anterior tilting on thoracic cage
Scapular elevation, downward rotation, and medial border lifting from thorax
Scapular depression, lateral winging, and downward spinning around clavicle
explanation: The Serratus Anterior pulls the scapula anterolaterally (protraction), rotates the inferior angle laterally (upward rotation), and holds the medial border against the thorax (posterior tilting), stabilizing the scapulothoracic joint.

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: In the functional anatomy of the knee joint, why is the Medial Meniscus significantly less mobile and more prone to injury than the Lateral Meniscus?
options: The medial meniscus has zero capsular attachments and floats freely in joint
The lateral meniscus carries 100% of all compressive loads during walking
The medial meniscus is composed purely of fragile elastic connective tissue
The medial meniscus is firmly anchored to deep MCL and capsule with less mobility
explanation: The medial meniscus has firm peripheral attachments to the joint capsule and deep medial collateral ligament (MCL), making it less mobile (~5 mm translation vs ~11 mm for lateral meniscus) and more vulnerable to shearing forces.

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: In hip biomechanics, what is the primary role of the Gluteus Medius muscle during single-leg stance?
options: Extending the lumbar spine into hyperlordosis and contralateral rotation
Concentric hip adduction pulling thighs together across anatomical midline
Generating an abductor moment to stabilize pelvis horizontally in stance
Flexing the knee joint to 90 degrees during the swing flight phase of gait
explanation: During single-leg stance, the stance gluteus medius contracts to create a powerful lateral abductor moment that counteracts body weight torque, maintaining a level pelvis and preventing contralateral pelvic drop.

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: In the upper extremity kinetic chain, what is the functional purpose of the 'Rotator Interval' in the glenohumeral joint?
options: A surgical incision created during total shoulder joint replacement surgery
A structural bone fracture line passing through surgical neck of humerus
An empty bursa space beneath deltoid tuberosity along lateral humerus
An anatomical space between supraspinatus and subscapularis containing CHL and LHB
explanation: The rotator interval is a triangular space bounded by the supraspinatus (superiorly) and subscapularis (inferiorly), reinforced by the coracohumeral and superior glenohumeral ligaments, stabilizing the biceps tendon and resisting inferior translation at 0° abduction.

subtopic: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Jacquelin Perry & Judith M. Burnfield
text: During the 'Mid-Stance' phase of normal walking, what is the primary mechanical function of the Soleus and Gastrocnemius muscle group?
options: Concentric explosive plantarflexion to launch the body forward into swing
Pure isometric contraction of the toe extensor tendons to clear the floor
Eccentric deceleration of forward tibial progression over the fixed foot
Passive complete relaxation allowing uncontrolled tibial collapse into flexion
explanation: In Mid-Stance, the calf plantarflexors (particularly soleus) contract eccentrically to restrain and control the rate of forward tibial advancement over the stationary planted foot, stabilizing the knee in extension.

subtopic: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Perry & Burnfield
text: A 'Genu Recurvatum' pathological gait pattern (knee hyperextension during stance) is commonly adopted as a compensation for:
options: Excessive strength and hyper-reflexia of the tibialis anterior dorsiflexor
Severe contracture of the hamstring muscles holding knee locked at 90 deg
Spasticity of the gluteus maximus extensor muscle belly during swing phase
Severe weakness or paralysis of the Quadriceps group, locking knee in extension
explanation: Patients with quadriceps weakness lack the active torque to control knee flexion during stance; they compensate by thrusting the knee into passive bony/ligamentous hyperextension (genu recurvatum) to keep the GRF anterior to the knee.

subtopic: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Perry & Burnfield
text: In 3D gait kinematic analysis, what is the 'Center of Pressure' (COP)?
options: The hydrostatic blood pressure recorded inside the popliteal artery in gait
The atmospheric barometric pressure recorded inside the motion laboratory
The point of application of resultant ground reaction force on foot sole
The center of mass of the human skull measured in quiet standing posture
explanation: Center of Pressure (COP) represents the spatial location of the centroid of total vertical ground reaction force exerted on the contact surface, progressing from heel strike along the lateral foot to the 1st/2nd metatarsal heads at toe-off.

subtopic: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Perry & Burnfield / Brukner & Khan
text: During high-speed running, during which phase of the sprint gait cycle is the risk of an acute Hamstring strain injury highest?
options: Mid-stance phase of single support when foot is flat on running surface
Early swing phase when knee is flexing to 90 degrees behind the hip joint
Mid-flight phase when both feet are suspended in air without contact
Late terminal swing phase during maximal eccentric lengthening deceleration
explanation: Biomechanical studies (Chumanov, Thelen et al.) show hamstring peak muscle-tendon length, high eccentric force, and negative work peak simultaneously during late terminal swing as the hamstrings decelerate the advancing shank.

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson
text: In therapeutic electrotherapy, the 'Strength-Duration Curve' illustrates that to depolarize a denervated muscle fiber directly (in the absence of intact motor nerves), the electrical stimulus requires:
options: High-frequency radio waves at 27 MHz without direct current component
A long pulse duration of 10–100 ms at significantly higher amplitude
A very short pulse duration of <0.1 ms at low sensory current threshold
A zero-second pulse duration of 0 ms as denervated fibers never fire
explanation: Denervated muscle lacks low-threshold nerve axons (chronaxie of nerve is ~0.05–0.1 ms; muscle membrane chronaxie is typically >10 ms), requiring long pulse durations, often 10–100 ms, and higher amplitudes to depolarize the sarcolemma directly.

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson
text: In Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation (NMES), what is the optimal pulse frequency range standardly selected to produce a smooth, tetanic muscle contraction?
options: 35 to 50 Hz, producing smooth fused contraction with manageable fatigue
500 to 1000 Hz, producing continuous rapid destruction and severe burns
1 to 5 Hz, producing isolated single twitches without any force fusion
0 to 0 Hz, as pulse frequency has zero effect on muscular contraction
explanation: A frequency of 35–50 pulses per second (Hz) produces complete physiological tetany (fused contraction) while minimizing rapid neuromuscular junction fatigue associated with higher frequencies (>80 Hz).

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson
text: In therapeutic phonophoresis, what is the physical mechanism by which ultrasound enhances the transdermal delivery of topical pharmacological agents (e.g., NSAIDs)?
options: Complete thermal ablation and vaporization of epidermis under ultrasound
Acoustic cavitation and microstreaming increasing stratum corneum permeability
Direct electrical attraction of positively charged ionic drug molecules
Freezing topical pharmacological creams into rigid subcutaneous crystals
explanation: Phonophoresis utilizes acoustic cavitation, acoustic microstreaming, and mild thermal effects to disrupt the lipid bilayer of the stratum corneum, increasing skin permeability for drug diffusion.

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson
text: Which electrophysical modality generates deep endogenous therapeutic tissue heating primarily through molecular dipole rotation and ionic conduction inside electrolyte-rich tissues?
options: Pulsed Ultrasound delivered at 3 MHz with 0.5 W/cm2 spatial intensity
Infrared Radiation therapy delivered at 1000 nm with 0.5 W/cm2 intensity
Continuous Shortwave Diathermy delivered at 27 MHz via dielectric heat
Ultraviolet Radiation therapy delivered at 250 nm with 0.5 W/cm2 intensity
explanation: Continuous SWD uses high-frequency electromagnetic fields (27.12 MHz) that cause rapid oscillation/dipole rotation of water molecules and ionic movement, producing uniform deep endogenous heat in muscular and vascular tissues.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In Vestibular Rehabilitation Therapy (VRT), what is the primary physiological mechanism targeted by 'Gaze Stability Exercises' (e.g., VOR x 1 and VOR x 2 viewing drills)?
options: Habituation exercises to exhaust otoconia particles in semi-canals
Canalith repositioning maneuvers to clear debris from cupula domes
Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex adaptation to maintain clear visual fixation
Continuous bed rest in darkened rooms to eliminate vestibular input
explanation: Gaze stability drills (VOR x 1 where head moves while staring at fixed letter; VOR x 2 where target and head move in opposite directions) induce vestibular neuroplastic adaptation and recalibrate the gain of the VOR.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In spinal cord injury functional assessment, the ASIA Impairment Scale (AIS) Grade 'C' is defined as:
options: Complete injury: no sensory or motor function remains in sacral S4–S5
Incomplete: sensory but not motor function is preserved below the neurological level
Incomplete motor injury; at least half of key muscles below the level are at least grade three
Incomplete motor injury; over half of key muscles below the level are below grade-three strength
explanation: AIS C is an incomplete motor injury in which more than half of the key muscles below the neurological level have a grade below 3/5. AIS D has at least half at grade 3/5 or higher.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In Parkinson's disease neurorehabilitation, what is the primary therapeutic rationale for utilizing 'Auditory and Visual Rhythmic Cuing' (e.g., metronome beat or floor laser lines) during gait training?
options: Cues stimulate dopamine synthesis in the substantia nigra pars compacta
Cues bypass basal ganglia by accessing cerebellar-premotor sensory loops
Cues exhaust motor unit action potential firing rates across all muscles
Cues induce permanent structural neuroplasticity in descending tracts
explanation: External rhythmic sensory cues (auditory metronome, visual step lines) bypass deficient basal ganglia internal rhythm generation, utilizing alternative cortical-cerebellar visual/auditory pathways to overcome freezing and hypokinesia.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In the management of spastic cerebral palsy or adult spasticity, what is the mechanism of action of intramuscular Botulinum Toxin Type A (Botox) injections?
options: Cleaving SNAP twenty-five to block acetylcholine release at the motor endplate
Directly blocking voltage-gated sodium channels along motor axon axons
Stimulating GABA-A receptors in the anterior horn cells of spinal cord
Mechanically denaturing actin-myosin cross-bridge proteins in sarcomeres
explanation: Botulinum toxin Type A cleaves SNAP-25, preventing presynaptic vesicular release of acetylcholine at the motor endplate, producing localized, dose-dependent chemical denervation lasting 3–4 months.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / McKenzie
text: In the McKenzie Method (MDT), an athlete who presents with a 'Lateral Shift' of the lumbar spine (lumbar listing) must have the lateral shift corrected:
options: After completing 6 weeks of aggressive high-load lumbar flexion drills
After passive mechanical traction has reduced the disc bulge completely
Concurrently while performing loaded rotation stretches on treatment mat
Before attempting extension as extension is blocked if shift remains
explanation: In MDT, an acute relevant lateral shift is a mechanical block; it MUST be manually corrected and centralized in the frontal plane before sagittal extension exercises can be successfully introduced.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / Butler
text: When performing Upper Limb Neurodynamic Testing for the Radial Nerve (ULTT 2b / Radial Bias), what is the standardized shoulder and arm movement sequence?
options: Shoulder depression, elbow flexion, external rotation, and forearm supination throughout the test
Shoulder elevation, elbow extension, lateral rotation, and wrist extension without pronation throughout the test
Shoulder abduction, elbow flexion, forearm supination, and wrist flexion without finger flexion throughout the test
Depress shoulder, extend elbow, internally rotate, pronate, flex wrist/fingers/thumb, then slightly abduct shoulder
explanation: Radial nerve bias (ULTT 2b) sequence: Shoulder girdle depression -> Elbow extension -> Shoulder internal rotation -> Forearm pronation -> Wrist/finger/thumb flexion -> Shoulder abduction (~10–30°).

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / Cyriax
text: In Cyriax's manual therapy framework, 'Deep Transverse Friction Massage' (DTFM) is specifically applied:
options: Strictly transverse to fiber orientation at the precise lesion site
Strictly parallel along the longitudinal direction of tendon fibers
Circular clockwise rubbing patterns over the surrounding muscle belly
Light superficial effleurage strokes without mobilizing deeper tissues
explanation: Cyriax DTFM is applied perpendicular (transverse) to the tendon/ligament fiber direction at the exact focal lesion site to produce transverse movement of collagen fibers, prevent abnormal cross-links, and induce hyperemic analgesia.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby
text: In the Kaltenborn manual therapy system, what is the 'Resting Position' (Loose-Packed Position) of a joint?
options: The position where capsule and ligaments have greatest laxity/joint play
The position where joint surfaces are fully congruent and capsule tight
The terminal end of available physiological active range of motion
The position of maximal joint compression under full body weight load
explanation: The loose-packed (resting) position is where articular surface congruency is minimal, joint capsule and ligaments are relaxed, joint volume is greatest, and joint play is maximal, making it the safest starting position for mobilization.

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: What is the Close-Packed Position of the Talocrural (Ankle) Joint where joint stability is maximal and articular surfaces are fully congruent?
options: Maximal ankle plantarflexion with posterior talar dome in mortise
Maximal ankle dorsiflexion with anterior talar dome wedged in mortise
Anatomical neutral zero degrees with foot in 10 degrees of inversion
Full subtalar eversion with midtarsal joint completely unlocked
explanation: At maximal dorsiflexion, the wider anterior portion of the talar trochlea is wedged tightly into the mortise between the malleoli, making it the close-packed position with maximal congruency and taut collateral ligaments.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / Mulligan
text: In Mulligan's concept for treating acute lateral ankle sprains with persistent dorsiflexion restriction and pain, what Mobilization with Movement (MWM) technique is applied?
options: Anterior glide of distal fibula maintained during passive plantarflexion
Lateral distraction of calcaneus maintained during seated leg curls
Posterior-superior fibular or posterior talar glide during a weight-bearing lunge
Pure inferior traction of talocrural joint held for thirty minutes
explanation: Mulligan's ankle MWM applies a posterior/superior glide to the distal fibula (or posterior talar glide) with a belt or hand while the patient performs an active weight-bearing forward lunge into previously painful dorsiflexion.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: In the cervical spine, the 'Sharp-Purser Test' is a specialized clinical safety test designed to evaluate the structural stability and integrity of which ligament?
options: Alar Ligaments evaluating rotational instability of atlantoaxial joint
Tectorial Membrane evaluating cranial separation from cervical spine
Transverse Ligament of Atlas evaluating atlantoaxial instability
Apical Ligament evaluating vertical odontoid displacement in canal
explanation: The Sharp-Purser test evaluates atlantoaxial instability (subluxation of atlas on axis from transverse ligament insufficiency, common in rheumatoid arthritis/trauma); a posterior translation/relocation clunk confirms transverse ligament laxity.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The 'Lachman Test' is the most sensitive clinical test for diagnosing acute Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) tears. What is the precise testing position and mechanical maneuver?
options: Patient supine, knee flexed to 90°, pulling proximal tibia forward
Patient supine, knee flexed to 25°, translating proximal tibia forward
Patient prone, knee flexed to 90°, applying axial compression with rot
Patient side-lying, knee in full extension at 0°, applying varus stress
explanation: The Lachman test (at 20°–30° knee flexion) relaxes the secondary hamstring/capsular restraints, isolating the anterior cruciate ligament. A soft/mushy end-point and anterior translation >3mm compared to the uninjured side confirms an ACL tear.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The 'Dial Test' (Tibial External Rotation Test) is positive when tibial external rotation increases by >10° compared to the contralateral normal limb. What do positive findings at 30° knee flexion versus 90° knee flexion differentiate?
options: Anterior cruciate tear at 30° flexion; medial meniscus tear at 90° flexion
Patellar subluxation at 30° flexion; quadriceps tendon tear at 90° flexion
Peroneal nerve entrapment at 30° flexion; tibial nerve injury at 90° flexion
30° only suggests isolated PLC injury; both 30° and 90° suggest combined PLC/PCL injury
explanation: Increased external rotation at 30° only indicates an isolated PLC injury (popliteus, LCL, popliteofibular ligament). Increased external rotation at both 30° and 90° confirms combined disruption of the PLC and PCL.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The 'Hawkins-Kennedy Test' for subacromial shoulder impingement is performed with the shoulder positioned in:
options: 90° of extension behind back with forearm held in maximal supination
90° forward flexion in scaption with forced passive internal rotation
90° pure coronal abduction with active external rotation on couch
90° abduction at the side with resisted isometric external rotation
explanation: Hawkins-Kennedy test involves flexing the arm to 90° in the scapular plane and forcefully internally rotating the humerus, driving the greater tuberosity and supraspinatus tendon against the coracoacromial arch.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The 'Finkelstein Test' is diagnostic for De Quervain's Tenosynovitis. What anatomical structures passing through the first dorsal extensor compartment of the wrist are stressed during this maneuver?
options: Extensor Digitorum and Extensor Indicis tendons over dorsum of wrist
Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus and Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis tendons
Flexor Carpi Radialis and Flexor Pollicis Longus tendons in carpal canal
Abductor Pollicis Longus and Extensor Pollicis Brevis tendons in sheath
explanation: Finkelstein's test (making a fist with the thumb tucked inside the fingers followed by passive ulnar deviation of the wrist) stretches the inflamed APL and EPB tendons within the first dorsal extensor compartment sheath.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee / Butler
text: In the differential diagnosis of lumbar radiculopathy, what constitutes a positive 'Slump Test' according to Maitland and Butler?
options: Reproduction of radicular pain in trunk/leg, relieved by neck extension
Painless restriction of lumbar spine extension in quiet standing posture
Immediate complete numbness of bilateral upper extremities during rotation
Audible popping in thoracic spine without any peripheral leg symptoms
explanation: A positive neurodynamic Slump test reproduces neurogenic symptoms with combined dural tension, and crucially, symptoms must modulate (ease) when releasing the sensitizing cervical flexion maneuver, confirming neural rather than muscular tension.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The Crank Test and O’Brien’s Active Compression Test assess which broad shoulder pathology, with O’Brien’s test sometimes used when SLAP pathology is suspected?
options: Rotator-cuff-related subacromial pain with painful arc
Glenoid labral pathology, possibly including a SLAP lesion
Anterior glenohumeral instability with apprehension
Adhesive capsulitis with restricted passive motion
explanation: These tests can contribute to assessment of glenoid labral pathology. Neither test alone establishes a specific SLAP tear.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The 'Noble Compression Test' is utilized in sports physical therapy to confirm the diagnosis of:
options: Iliotibial Band Friction over femoral epicondyle at 30° knee flexion
Medial meniscus tear over femoral condyle cartilage at 30° knee flexion
Plantaris muscle tendon rupture in calf compartment at 30° knee flexion
Pes Anserine bursitis over proximal tibial bone at 30° knee flexion
explanation: Noble's compression test applies digital pressure over the lateral femoral epicondyle while passively extending the knee from 90°; severe pain reproduction at ~30° flexion (where the ITB impinges over the epicondyle) is diagnostic.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: The 'Squeeze Test' (Hopkins Test) of the lower leg, where the fibula and tibia are compressed together at mid-calf, is positive for:
options: High Ankle Sprain of the distal tibiofibular syndesmotic ligament
Complete avulsion fracture of navicular tuberosity in medial midfoot
Plantar fascia microtears at calcaneal medial tubercle insertion site
Isolated superficial tear of the anterior talofibular ligament joint
explanation: Compressing the tibia and fibula at the mid-calf separates the distal tibiofibular joint; pain reproduction at the distal syndesmosis indicates syndesmotic sprain (AITFL, PITFL, interosseous membrane).

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby
text: In the Delorme and Watkins Progressive Resistive Exercise (PRE) protocol, how are the 3 sets of 10 repetitions structured based on the 10-Repetition Maximum (10RM)?
options: Set 1 at 100% of 10RM, Set 2 at 75% of 10RM, and Set 3 at 50% of 10RM in gym
Set 1 at 10% of 10RM, Set 2 at 20% of 10RM, and Set 3 at 30% of 10RM in gym
All 3 sets performed strictly at 100% of 1RM to absolute muscular failure
Set 1 at 50% of 10RM, Set 2 at 75% of 10RM, and Set 3 at 100% of 10RM in gym
explanation: The DeLorme PRE protocol utilizes progressive warm-up/overload: Set 1 = 10 reps @ 50% 10RM, Set 2 = 10 reps @ 75% 10RM, and Set 3 = 10 reps @ 100% 10RM. The Oxford technique inverts this sequence.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise - Kisner & Colby / Brukner & Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
text: In the management of mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, what are the precise parameters of the 'Alfredson Eccentric Loading Protocol'?
options: 3 sets of 15 straight-knee and 3 sets of 15 bent-knee reps, twice daily
100 continuous rapid concentric jumps performed on a trampoline weekly
1 set of 5 repetitions performed once weekly on a leg press machine load
Passive calf stretching held continuously for 45 minutes twice per day
explanation: Alfredson's eccentric protocol mandates 3x15 reps with knee straight (gastrocnemius focus) and 3x15 with knee bent (soleus focus), completed 2x/day, 7 days/week for 12 weeks, loading through mild tendon pain.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby
text: In manual therapy according to Maitland, what defines a 'Grade IV' joint mobilization technique?
options: A large-amplitude rhythmic oscillatory movement performed within range
A small-amplitude rhythmic oscillatory movement performed at beginning
A small-amplitude oscillatory movement at end of range into resistance
A high-velocity thrust manipulation performed at the physiological limit
explanation: Maitland Grade IV is a small-amplitude oscillation performed at the end of the available range (into tissue resistance/stiffness). Grade I is small amplitude at start; Grade II is large in mid-range; Grade III is large into resistance; Grade V is high-velocity thrust.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby
text: In Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF), the 'Hold-Relax with Agonist Contraction' (HR-AC) stretching technique utilizes which two neurological mechanisms simultaneously to maximize muscle relaxation?
options: Reciprocal inhibition caused only by a rapid stretch reflex
Presynaptic inhibition caused only by cutaneous receptors
Pharmacological blockade of acetylcholine at the motor endplate
GTO-mediated autogenic inhibition plus Ia-mediated reciprocal inhibition
explanation: Hold-relax with agonist contraction combines GTO-mediated autogenic inhibition from the isometric hold of the tight muscle with Ia-mediated reciprocal inhibition when the opposing agonist contracts. It does not discharge muscle spindles as the primary mechanism.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise - Kisner & Colby / Rio et al.
text: In knee rehabilitation, why is the 'Spanish Squat' (isometric squatting against a rigid looped strap anchored behind the proximal calves) biomechanically preferred for patellar tendinopathy?
options: The strap maintains vertical tibia, reducing patellofemoral compressive peak
The strap eliminates all quadriceps muscle firing to rest tendon completely
The strap forces the knee into extreme hyperextension during seated holds
The strap increases anterior tibial shear forces to accelerate ligament repair
explanation: The Spanish squat uses a non-compliant strap behind the proximal tibia, allowing the athlete to sit back into a vertical-shank squat (~70°–90° knee flexion), producing high quadriceps tendon tension with low patellofemoral contact pressure.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / McKenzie
text: In the McKenzie Method (Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy - MDT), what clinical phenomenon confirms a 'Derangement Syndrome' that is responding favorably to directional preference exercises?
options: Centralization of radiating symptoms moving toward the spinal midline
Peripheralization of sharp pain radiating further down into foot toes
Complete structural ossification of the lumbar intervertebral disc ring
Instantaneous resolution of lumbar lordosis into rigid spinal kyphosis
explanation: Centralization is the hallmark of MDT derangement reduction: distal radiating/referred pain abolishes in a distal-to-proximal sequence toward the midline in response to directional loading (e.g., repeated extension).

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: In kinesiology, what is the 'Convex-Concave Rule' (Freddy Kaltenborn) for the Glenohumeral Joint during active shoulder abduction?
options: The convex humeral head glides superiorly on concave glenoid fossa
The convex humeral head rolls inferiorly and glides inferiorly together
The concave glenoid fossa rolls superiorly on fixed convex humeral head
The convex humeral head rolls superiorly and glides inferiorly in fossa
explanation: According to Kaltenborn's rule, when a convex joint surface moves on a concave fixed surface, roll and slide occur in OPPOSITE directions. In shoulder abduction, the convex humeral head rolls superiorly and slides inferiorly.

subtopic: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Jacquelin Perry & Judith M. Burnfield
text: In the biomechanics of human gait, what constitutes the 'First Ankle Rocker' (Heel Rocker) during the initial contact phase?
options: Concentric contraction of gastrocnemius to propel the leg forward in gait
Passive elastic recoil of the Achilles tendon without active muscle work
Isometric contraction of intrinsic foot muscles to lock the tarsal joints
Deceleration of foot drop controlled by eccentric tibialis anterior pull
explanation: The 1st rocker (heel rocker) occurs from heel strike to foot flat; the heel acts as a pivot and the pretibial muscles (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus) contract eccentrically to decelerate foot slap and pull the tibia forward.
