subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: During normal human gait, what is the primary kinematic function of the 'Screw-Home Mechanism' of the knee joint during the terminal 30° of extension?
options: The femur rotates externally 10° on the fixed tibia in closed kinetic chain
The patella translates medially 10° into the intercondylar groove on knee
The meniscus slides anteriorly 10° to completely block further motion
The tibia rotates externally 10° on fixed femur, locking knee in extension
explanation: The screw-home mechanism involves ~10° of tibial external rotation on the femur during terminal extension (driven by the shape of the medial femoral condyle and ACL tension), locking the knee for stable single-leg weight bearing.

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Jacquelin Perry & Judith M. Burnfield
text: A 'Trendelenburg Gait' (uncompensated) is characterized by a pelvic drop on the CONTRALATERAL (swing) side during single-leg stance, caused by weakness of which muscle?
options: Adductor Longus and Gracilis of the contralateral swing limb during gait
Iliopsoas and Rectus Femoris of the ipsilateral stance limb during gait
Gluteus Medius and Minimus of the ipsilateral stance leg during gait
Tensor Fasciae Latae and Sartorius of the contralateral swing limb in gait
explanation: Weakness of the stance-limb hip abductors (gluteus medius/minimus) prevents generation of adequate abductor torque to keep the pelvis level, allowing the unsupported contralateral pelvis to drop (positive Trendelenburg).

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: In the foot and ankle kinetic chain, what is the 'Windlass Mechanism' described by J.H. Hicks?
options: Plantarflexion of the hallux relaxes the plantar aponeurosis during push-off
Eversion of the subtalar joint unlocks the midtarsal joints for push-off
Hallux dorsiflexion tightens plantar fascia, elevating medial arch lever
Inversion of the calcaneus completely flattens the longitudinal arch
explanation: Hicks' Windlass Mechanism: big toe extension in late stance winds the plantar fascia around the 1st MTP head, shortening the distance between calcaneus and metatarsals, elevating the arch and rigidifying the midfoot for propulsion.

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: In shoulder kinesiology, what is the normal physiological 'Scapulohumeral Rhythm' ratio during full arm elevation (abduction or flexion)?
options: 1:2 overall ratio (2° scapulothoracic motion for every 1° glenohumeral)
2:1 overall ratio (2° glenohumeral motion for every 1° scapulothoracic)
5:1 overall ratio (5° glenohumeral motion for every 1° scapulothoracic)
1:1 overall ratio (identical equal angular motion at both articulations)
explanation: Codman and Inman established the 2:1 scapulohumeral rhythm: 180° of shoulder elevation consists of ~120° glenohumeral motion and ~60° scapulothoracic upward rotation.

subtopic: Gait Analysis: Normal and Pathological Function - Jacquelin Perry & Judith M. Burnfield
text: During the 'Loading Response' (Weight Acceptance) phase of gait, what is the primary functional role of the Quadriceps Femoris muscle group?
options: Concentric contraction to accelerate knee into terminal hyperextension
Isometric contraction to lock the tibiofemoral joint in rigid extension
Eccentric contraction to absorb impact shock and control knee flexion
Passive relaxation allowing ground reaction forces alone to stabilize
explanation: In Loading Response (initial double support), the quadriceps contract eccentrically to control knee flexion to ~15°–18°, shock-absorbing ground impact forces and maintaining postural stability.

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann / Wilk et al.
text: In the biomechanics of pitching and throwing, during which phase is the anterior glenohumeral joint capsule and the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) subjected to maximal tensile stress?
options: Late Cocking to Early Acceleration phase with maximal valgus torque
Wind-up phase before the lead leg lifts off the pitching rubber mound
Follow-through phase when the throwing arm crosses the contralateral knee
Deceleration phase after the ball has completely left the pitcher's hand
explanation: Late cocking/early acceleration involves extreme humeral external rotation (up to 170°+) and high angular velocity, generating peak anterior glenohumeral shear and massive medial elbow valgus torque on the UCL.

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson
text: In therapeutic electrotherapy, according to the 'Gate Control Theory of Pain' (Melzack & Wall), how does conventional High-Frequency TENS (80–120 Hz) produce analgesia?
options: Directly depolarizing unmyelinated C fibers to destroy peripheral pain paths
Selectively stimulating large A-beta fibers to inhibit nociceptive inputs
Inducing severe thermal coagulative necrosis across superficial skin nerves
Stimulating the pituitary gland to release adrenocorticotropic hormones
explanation: Conventional TENS utilizes high frequency (80–120 Hz) and low pulse duration (<100 microseconds) at sensory intensity to activate A-beta fibers, closing the spinal gate in the substantia gelatinosa to inhibit incoming nociceptive input.

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson
text: In therapeutic ultrasound, what is the significance of the 'Beam Non-Uniformity Ratio' (BNR)?
options: The ratio of crystal surface area to soundhead geometric housing area
The percentage of electrical power converted into audible acoustic waves
The ratio of peak spatial intensity to average spatial intensity across face
The total depth of acoustic penetration measured in centimeters in tissue
explanation: BNR reflects ultrasound beam quality (Spatial Peak Intensity / Spatial Average Intensity). Lower BNR (closer to 1:1, clinically <5:1 or <3:1) delivers uniform acoustic energy without dangerous focal hot spots that cause periosteal pain.

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson
text: In electrotherapy, why is 'Interferential Current' (IFC) able to penetrate deeper into biological tissues with less skin discomfort than standard low-frequency currents?
options: Using medium-frequency carrier currents to reduce capacitive impedance
IFC uses radioactive isotopes that pass freely through adipose tissue
Medium-frequency waves completely paralyze cutaneous sensory receptors
Interferential currents deliver high-voltage direct galvanic current
explanation: Skin impedance is inversely proportional to frequency. Medium-frequency carrier waves (~4000 Hz) encounter low capacitive skin resistance, crossing painlessly to intersect at depth where they produce a low-frequency therapeutic beat current.

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson / Rompe et al.
text: In the application of Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy (ESWT) for chronic recalcitrant plantar fasciitis, what is the primary biological mechanism of action?
options: Freezing the subcalcaneal bursa into solid ice crystals to stop metabolism
Acoustic microtrauma stimulating mechanotransduction and VEGF synthesis
Direct electrical stimulation of tibial nerve to paralyze intrinsic foot
Thermal ablation and complete vaporization of inflamed plantar fascia tissue
explanation: ESWT delivers acoustic shockwaves that trigger cellular mechanotransduction, release growth factors (VEGF, PCNA, eNOS), stimulate microvascular neovascularization, and deplete substance P in nociceptors.

subtopic: Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice - Tim Watson
text: In Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation (NMES) for quadriceps arthrogenic muscle inhibition post-ACL reconstruction, what 'Russian Current' parameters are traditionally used (Kots protocol)?
options: Single pulse micro-current at 1 Hz in 50 bursts/sec at sensory threshold
Continuous direct galvanic current at 100 mA in 50 bursts/sec for duty
2500 Hz medium-frequency sine wave in 50 bursts/sec on 10s/50s duty
High-frequency radio waves at 27 MHz in 50 bursts/sec without duty
explanation: Kots' Russian current utilizes a 2500 Hz carrier frequency modulated into 50 Hz burst frequency (10 ms burst, 10 ms inter-burst interval), applied with a 1:5 duty cycle (10s on, 50s off) to elicit maximal tetanic recruitment.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In neuro-rehabilitation, 'Constraint-Induced Movement Therapy' (CIMT - Edward Taub) is founded on which neuroplastic principle?
options: Eliminating all active motor practice and relying purely on sensory current
Using full-body hypnosis to restore cortical representation without motion
Overcoming Learned Non-Use by restraining unaffected limb in CIMT training
Applying continuous passive motion to unaffected arm while paretic is still
explanation: CIMT reverses 'learned non-use' in stroke/hemiparesis by restraining the sound limb (e.g., in a mitt for 90% of waking hours) while engaging the affected limb in intensive, repetitive, shaped functional tasks.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In the Bobath Concept (Neuro-Developmental Treatment - NDT), what is the primary focus of handling and therapeutic facilitation?
options: Inhibiting abnormal tone and synergies while facilitating postural control
Encouraging heavy ballistic maximum resistance training using mass synergy
Relying exclusively on passive mechanical stretching on a motorized couch
Immobilizing all functional joints in rigid plaster casts to prevent contract
explanation: Bobath NDT emphasizes dynamic handling at key points of control to inhibit spasticity/primitive mass synergies, optimize biomechanical alignment, and facilitate active selective motor patterns.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In Brunnstrom's Stages of Motor Recovery following stroke, what characterizes 'Stage 3'?
options: Stage 1: Severe flaccidity with complete absence of voluntary motor action
Stage 6: Complete return of fine motor coordination and movement speed
Stage 3: Spasticity peaks and basic voluntary movement synergies appear
Stage 4: Spasticity begins declining and isolated movements are normal
explanation: Brunnstrom Stage 3: Spasticity reaches its maximum severity, and the patient gains voluntary control over the basic limb synergies (movement occurs only within stereotypical mass flexor or extensor synergies).

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In Frenkel's Exercises for sensory cerebellar ataxia, what sensory system is deliberately utilized to compensate for impaired proprioception?
options: Visual tracking and conscious visual control of foot placement on targets
Vestibular caloric stimulation using iced water irrigations of the ear canal
Thermal skin receptors stimulated with continuous superficial ice massage
Complete sensory deprivation with eyes blindfolded and ears muffled in room
explanation: Frenkel's exercises use conscious visual attention, concentration, and repetition to compensate for lost proprioceptive feedback, retraining coordination through precise limb placement on marked boards/lines.

subtopic: Physical Rehabilitation - Susan B. O'Sullivan & Thomas J. Schmitz
text: In autonomic dysfunction following spinal cord injury at or above T6, what life-threatening medical emergency is triggered by noxious stimuli below the lesion level?
options: Diabetic ketoacidosis caused by acute destruction of the endocrine pancreas
Orthostatic Hypotension with sudden profound blood pressure drop on standing
Autonomic Dysreflexia with severe hypertension, headache, and sweating
Acute heat stroke accompanied by complete cessation of cranial nerve output
explanation: Autonomic Dysreflexia (in T6 and above injuries) is triggered by noxious visceral/cutaneous stimuli (e.g., full bladder, fecal impaction). Unchecked sympathetic reflex causes severe hypertension, dangerous intracranial hemorrhage, and reflex bradycardia.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / Butler
text: When performing Upper Limb Neurodynamic Testing for the Median Nerve (ULTT 1 / Median Nerve Bias), what is the correct anatomical test sequence?
options: Shoulder extension behind back with elbow at 90° and finger adduction
Shoulder depression, 110° ABD, ER, supination, wrist/finger/elbow ext
Shoulder elevation, adduction at 90°, internal rotation, wrist flex
Shoulder abduction to 90° with maximal elbow flexion, pronation, wrist
explanation: ULTT 1 (Median nerve bias) sequence: Shoulder girdle depression -> Shoulder abduction (~110°) -> Shoulder external rotation -> Forearm supination -> Wrist/finger/thumb extension -> Elbow extension -> Sensitization with contralateral cervical side-bend.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / Magee
text: When performing the Slump Test, if knee extension is limited and painful, what sensitizing maneuver differentiates neural dural tension from hamstring muscular tightness?
options: Releasing hip flexion while keeping the cervical spine fixed
Changing only the knee angle while keeping the neural interfaces unchanged
Releasing cervical flexion; symptom change supports neural mechanosensitivity
Applying ice to the hamstring while keeping all neural positions unchanged
explanation: Cervical release can serve as structural differentiation because it changes neural-tissue loading without materially changing hamstring length. Symptom change supports neural mechanosensitivity but does not alone confirm a specific nerve lesion.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / Kisner & Colby
text: In the manual therapy management of an adhesive capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder) with severe restriction of external rotation and abduction, what glenohumeral mobilization glides are indicated?
options: Anterior glide for external rotation plus inferior glide for elevation, selected for the restriction
Continuous axial compression into the glenoid without a directional glide or movement-specific aim
A superior glide into the coracoacromial arch without addressing the restricted joint movement
A high-velocity thrust into forced adduction and internal rotation without graded mobilization
explanation: Accessory-glide direction should follow the restricted movement and joint mechanics. An anterior glide is commonly used to improve external rotation, while an inferior glide can assist elevation; mobilization is individualized.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / Cyriax
text: In Cyriax's orthopedic framework, which clinical sign indicates a 'Contractile Tissue' lesion (muscle or tendon) rather than an inert tissue lesion?
options: Pain on active and passive movement in identical direction with zero lag
Painless active and passive range of motion across all planes in clinic
Pain on ACTIVE one way, PASSIVE opposite way, and on RESISTED contraction
Constant numbness and paresthesia unrelated to active muscular contraction
explanation: Cyriax established that contractile lesions produce pain when active contraction contracts the muscle or passive stretch lengthens it (opposite directions), and show pain/weakness during resisted isometric testing (which stresses contractile units without joint motion).

subtopic: Kinesiology of the Musculoskeletal System - Donald A. Neumann
text: What is the Close-Packed Position of the Glenohumeral Joint where joint congruency is maximal and capsuloligamentous structures are maximally taut?
options: 90° shoulder abduction combined with maximal external rotation on couch
0° adduction at side with 45° internal rotation on treatment couch
90° forward flexion with maximal internal rotation on treatment couch
90° scaption with neutral forearm rotation on treatment examination table
explanation: The close-packed position of the glenohumeral joint is full abduction and external rotation (the 90/90 or cocking position), where the joint surfaces are most congruent and the inferior glenohumeral ligament complex is taut.

subtopic: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Conditions - Prof. P.P. Mohanty / Mulligan
text: In Mulligan's concept, what are the primary principles of applying 'Mobilizations with Movement' (MWM)?
options: Applying sustained pain-free glide while patient performs active motion
Applying high-force painful manipulations through structural end barriers
Performing passive anatomical stretching only under general anesthesia
Immobilizing the joint in a plaster splint while applying electrical stim
explanation: Mulligan's MWM principles: PILL (Pain-free, Instant result, Long-Lasting). The therapist maintains a sustained passive accessory glide while the patient performs the active movement without any pain.

subtopic: Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques - Carolyn Kisner & Lynn Allen Colby / Hodges
text: In spinal rehabilitation, which deep core local stabilizing muscles exhibit delayed onset and selective atrophy following an initial episode of acute low back pain?
options: Transversus Abdominis and Lumbar Multifidus (deep local stabilizing system)
Rectus Abdominis and External Oblique (global superficial torque producers)
Latissimus Dorsi and Iliopsoas (superficial spinal extensor muscle complex)
Quadratus Lumborum and Psoas Major (lateral spinal torque stabilizers)
explanation: Hodges and Richardson demonstrated that low back pain induces motor control impairment and selective atrophy in the deep local stabilizers (Transversus Abdominis and Multifidus), which fail to automatically recover without targeted motor retraining.

subtopic: Orthopedic Physical Assessment - David J. Magee
text: In the cervical spine, what constitutes a positive 'Spurling's Test' (Foraminal Compression Test) for cervical radiculopathy?
options: Reproduction of radicular arm pain with extension, side-bend, axial load
Relief of neck pain when patient places hand on top of head in sitting
Reproduction of sharp dizziness when rapidly turning head to left side
Loss of radial pulse when turning head away from tested shoulder joint
explanation: Spurling's test narrows the neural foramen on the ipsilateral side (extension, ipsilateral lateral flexion, and axial downward pressure). Reproduction of shooting radicular arm pain is highly specific for cervical nerve root impingement.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Pivot-Shift Test' for anterior cruciate ligament deficiency evaluates dynamic rotary instability of the knee. What joint motions and translations occur during a positive test?
options: With the knee in full extension, applying axial compression completely dislocates the patella laterally
A positive test shows anterior-lateral tibial subluxation with valgus and internal rotation, then reduction
With the knee in prone 90° flexion, applying external rotation locks the popliteus tendon against the femur
With the knee in 90° flexion, applying varus stress forces the medial meniscus out of the joint space
explanation: MacIntosh Pivot-Shift: In extension/early flexion, valgus force + internal rotation causes the lateral tibial plateau to subluxate anteriorly. At ~30°–40° flexion, the IT band shifts from an extensor to a flexor, snapping the tibia back into anatomical reduction.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Posterior Sag Sign' (Godfrey's 90-90 Test) is diagnostic for rupture of which knee ligament?
options: Patellar tendon causing proximal migration of the patella into the thigh
The PCL is tested by observing posterior tibial sag with the hips and knees flexed
Medial collateral ligament causing opening of the medial joint space
Anterior cruciate ligament causing anterior tibial displacement
explanation: In Godfrey's 90-90 test (patient supine with hips and knees at 90° supported at the heels), gravity pulls the unsupported tibia posteriorly. A posterior step-off/sag confirms loss of PCL structural integrity.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Neer Impingement Test' is performed to identify subacromial shoulder impingement by:
options: The Neer test stabilizes the scapula while passively elevating the internally rotated arm
Adducting the arm across the chest while palpating the sternoclavicular articulation
Abducting the arm to 90° with maximal external rotation and applying axial distraction
Placing the hand behind the lower back and lifting the hand off the lumbar spine
explanation: Neer's test: the examiner stabilizes the scapular posture and passively elevates the arm into full overhead forward flexion while holding the shoulder in internal rotation, impinging the supraspinatus against the coracoacromial arch.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Speed's Test' and 'Yergason's Test' are classic orthopedic physical assessment tests used to diagnose pathology of the:
options: Coracobrachialis muscle origin at the coracoid process
Triceps brachii tendon insertion at the olecranon tip
They assess long-head biceps tendon pathology at the shoulder
Flexor carpi ulnaris tendon at the pisiform bone
explanation: Speed's test (resisted shoulder flexion with elbow extended and forearm supinated) and Yergason's test (resisted forearm supination and external rotation) stress the long head of the biceps brachii tendon within the intertubercular groove.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Straight Leg Raise' (SLR / Lasegue's Test) is positive for lower lumbar nerve root compromise (L4, L5, S1) when radicular pain is reproduced in which angular range of hip flexion?
options: It is positive when mid-range hip flexion reproduces radicular pain
Between 0° and 15° of hip flexion, reflecting hamstring slack
Between 85° and 110° of hip flexion, reflecting hip capsular end-feel
Only when the leg is hyperextended backwards into 30° of extension
explanation: In the SLR test, sciatic nerve roots undergo maximal traction and excursion through the neural foramina between 35° and 70° of hip flexion. Pain below 35° or above 70° typically reflects hip pathology or hamstring tightness.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'FABER' (Patrick's Test - Flexion, Abduction, External Rotation) is designed to screen for pathology in which joint complex?
options: Radiocarpal joint of the distal wrist
FABER screens the hip and sacroiliac joint
Proximal superior tibiofibular joint of the knee
Acromioclavicular joint of the shoulder girdle
explanation: In Patrick's FABER test (foot of involved leg placed on contralateral knee, pressing down on involved knee), pain in the anterior groin indicates hip pathology, while posterior pain indicates sacroiliac joint dysfunction.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Anterior Drawer Test' of the Ankle evaluates the structural integrity of which primary lateral ligament?
options: It assesses the ATFL for excessive anterior talar translation
Deltoid Ligament complex on the medial side of the ankle
Posterior talofibular ligament resisting extreme dorsiflexion
Calcaneofibular ligament resisting pure inversion in dorsiflexion
explanation: The ankle anterior drawer test (talus pulled forward relative to the stabilized tibia in ~10°–20° plantarflexion) isolates and strains the ATFL, the most frequently injured ligament in inversion ankle sprains.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Tinel's Sign' at the wrist produces tingling and paresthesia in the median nerve sensory distribution when:
options: Tinel sign is elicited by gentle percussion over the volar carpal tunnel
The ulnar nerve is compressed behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus
The hand is immersed in warm water for 15 consecutive minutes
The radial styloid process is forcefully sheared against the scaphoid bone
explanation: Tinel's sign: tapping over the volar carpal tunnel generates radiating paresthesias in the median nerve distribution (digits 1–3 and radial half of 4), indicating regenerating or compressed nerve axons.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In the Oxford Resistance Training protocol (Zinovieff), how are the 3 sets of 10 repetitions structured based on the 10RM?
options: All 3 sets performed strictly with 1 kg dumbbells regardless of patient strength
Set 1 at 50% of 10RM, Set 2 at 75% of 10RM, and Set 3 at 100% of 10RM
Performing 100 repetitions continuously without rest until muscular exhaustion
Oxford training uses descending loads: 100% of 10RM, then 75%, then 50%
explanation: The Oxford technique reverses DeLorme's protocol: Set 1 = 10 reps @ 100% 10RM, Set 2 = 10 reps @ 75% 10RM, Set 3 = 10 reps @ 50% 10RM, decreasing resistance as muscle fatigue accumulates.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In the Heavy Slow Resistance (HSR) protocol for patellar tendinopathy (Kongsgaard et al.), what training parameters are prescribed?
options: 100 rapid jumping jacks performed daily on a hard wooden floor
HSR uses slow progressive leg loading with several sets each week
Low-load isometric knee extensions performed at 10% 1RM for 1 repetition per day
Passive quadriceps stretching held for 10 minutes twice monthly
explanation: Kongsgaard's HSR protocol: 3 exercises (squat, leg press, hack squat) 3x/week; 4 sets progressing from 15RM down to 6RM with slow 6s repetition cadence (3s eccentric, 3s concentric), yielding high collagen turnover and clinical efficacy.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In manual therapy according to Maitland, what defines a 'Grade I' joint mobilization technique?
options: A high-velocity, small-amplitude thrust performed at anatomical end-range
A large-amplitude rhythmic oscillation moving deep into tissue resistance
Grade I uses small oscillations at the beginning of range to reduce pain
A sustained mechanical distraction of the joint held for 30 minutes continuously
explanation: Maitland Grade I is a small-amplitude oscillation near the starting position of range, free from tissue resistance. It stimulates mechanoreceptors to modulate pain via gate-control mechanisms without stretching capsule.

subtopic: Therapeutic exercise protocols and manual therapy
text: In PNF stretching, the 'Contract-Relax' (CR) technique achieves target muscle relaxation primarily through which neurophysiological reflex?
options: Reciprocal inhibition relaxes the antagonist when the opposing muscle contracts
The stretch reflex increases tension when a muscle is lengthened rapidly
A drug-induced block of acetylcholine prevents normal neuromuscular transmission
It uses target-muscle isometric contraction, relaxation, and subsequent stretching
explanation: Contract-relax uses an isometric contraction of the target tight muscle, followed by relaxation and stretching. GTO-mediated autogenic inhibition is one proposed neurophysiological contribution.

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In tendon rehabilitation, what is the 'Cook and Purdam Continuum Model of Tendon Pathology'?
options: It progresses from reactive tendinopathy through dysrepair to degeneration, guiding load management
A scoring system measuring the scale body weight of endurance distance runners
A classification system dividing bone fractures into transverse, oblique, and spiral patterns
A theoretical model stating that all tendon injuries require immediate surgical repair within 24 hours
explanation: Cook and Purdam's continuum categorizes tendon pathology into: 1. Reactive tendinopathy (acute non-inflammatory proliferative response), 2. Tendon dysrepair, and 3. Degenerative tendinopathy (extensive cell death/matrix breakdown).

subtopic: Therapeutic exercise protocols and manual therapy
text: In the McKenzie Method (MDT), what defines the 'Postural Syndrome' of spinal pain?
options: Pain caused by anatomical rupture of the annulus fibrosus and nucleus pulposus extrusion
It is pain from sustained postural loading of normal tissues that eases with correction
Pain caused by bony fracture of the vertebral body following high-impact trauma
Pain caused by severe systemic bacterial infection of the spinal cord meninges
explanation: Postural Syndrome in MDT results from sustained end-range mechanical stress on normal tissues (e.g., slouched sitting). It causes no ROM loss or deformity, and pain is instantly relieved by assuming correct neutral alignment.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In kinesiology, what is the 'Convex-Concave Rule' for the Tibiofemoral Joint of the knee during open-chain active knee extension?
options: The tibia undergoes pure linear translation without any rotational rolling movement
The concave tibial plateau rolls anteriorly and glides posteriorly in the opposite direction
The convex femoral condyles roll posteriorly and glide anteriorly on the fixed tibia
The concave tibia rolls and glides anteriorly on the fixed femur during extension
explanation: In open-chain knee extension, the concave tibia moves on the fixed convex femur. According to Kaltenborn's rule, when a concave surface moves on a convex surface, roll and slide occur in the SAME direction (both anteriorly).

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In gait analysis, what constitutes the 'Second Ankle Rocker' (Ankle Rocker) during the Mid-Stance phase?
options: The tibia advances over the planted foot under eccentric calf control
Explosive push-off from the forefoot driven by the flexor hallucis longus
Initial impact of the calcaneus on the ground controlled by the tibialis anterior
Passive elevation of the toes during the middle of the swing flight phase
explanation: The 2nd rocker (ankle rocker) occurs during Mid-Stance as the foot is flat on the ground and the tibia advances forward over the talus, restrained eccentrically by the soleus/gastrocnemius to control knee stability.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In lower extremity kinesiology, what is the role of the 'Popliteus' muscle during the initiation of knee flexion from a fully locked extension position in closed chain?
options: It plantarflexes the ankle joint to propel the foot off the ground
It forcefully locks the knee into hyperextension by pulling the patella superiorly
The popliteus unlocks the knee and retracts the lateral meniscus
It extends the hip joint to 90° during the mid-swing phase of running
explanation: The popliteus unlocks the screw-home mechanism: in weight-bearing (closed chain), it externally rotates the femur on the fixed tibia; in open chain, it internally rotates the tibia on the femur, while pulling the lateral meniscus posteriorly.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: A 'Steppage Gait' (Foot Drop Gait) is characterized by excessive hip and knee flexion during the swing phase to clear the toes, caused by paralysis or weakness of which nerve and muscle group?
options: Femoral Nerve and the quadriceps femoris muscle belly
Obturator Nerve and the hip adductor longus muscle
Peroneal nerve dysfunction causing weak ankle dorsiflexion
Tibial nerve and the ankle plantarflexors, gastrocnemius and soleus
explanation: Steppage gait results from common/deep peroneal nerve palsy causing tibialis anterior weakness (foot drop). The patient excessively flexes the hip and knee during swing to prevent the dragging toes from catching the ground.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In the foot and ankle complex, what occurs at the Midtarsal (Chopart's) Joint when the Subtalar Joint SUPINATES during the terminal stance/push-off phase of gait?
options: The plantar fascia completely tears away from the calcaneal tuberosity
The navicular bone completely dislocates superiorly out of the tarsal arch
Subtalar supination makes the midtarsal axes converge, locking the midfoot into a rigid lever
The axes become parallel, unlocking the midfoot to allow maximal flexibility and shock absorption
explanation: Subtalar supination crosses (converges) the axes of the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints, rigidifying the transverse tarsal joint into a stiff lever for efficient forward propulsion during push-off.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: In scapulothoracic kinematics, which muscle 'Force Couple' produces smooth upward rotation of the scapula during overhead arm elevation?
options: Rhomboid Major, Rhomboid Minor, and Levator Scapulae
Teres Major, Deltoid, and Coracobrachialis
Pectoralis Minor, Latissimus Dorsi, and Subscapularis
Upper Trapezius, Lower Trapezius, and Serratus Anterior
explanation: Scapular upward rotation is driven by a coordinated force couple: the Upper Trapezius pulls the clavicle/acromion superiorly, the Lower Trapezius pulls the medial spine inferiorly, and the Serratus Anterior pulls the inferior angle laterally.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: During the 'Terminal Stance' phase of walking gait, what is the primary mechanical event and muscle activation pattern occurring at the ankle?
options: Subtalar joint pronates maximally to flatten the medial arch completely
Terminal stance raises the heel while calf plantarflexors stabilize the forefoot
Heel strikes the ground with maximal tibialis anterior eccentric deceleration
Knee flexes to 60° while the foot is completely unloaded in the air
explanation: Terminal Stance begins with heel rise (3rd rocker/forefoot rocker): body weight rolls over the metatarsophalangeal joints, driven by powerful calf plantarflexor torque to stabilize the forefoot and prepare for push-off.

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Joint biomechanics, muscle levers and force couples
text: In shoulder biomechanics, what is the essential function of the 'Rotator Cuff Force Couple' (Subscapularis anteriorly, Infraspinatus/Teres Minor posteriorly) during arm abduction?
options: Completely relaxing the shoulder capsule to allow inferior humeral subluxation
Locking the glenohumeral joint in 90° of rigid internal rotation throughout elevation
The rotator cuff compresses and centers the humeral head, opposing the deltoid's upward shear
Pulling the humeral head superiorly into the subacromial arch to impinge the bursa
explanation: The deltoid creates a strong superior translatory shear vector during early abduction. The rotator cuff force couple exerts an inferior and compressive vector, centering the humeral head within the glenoid and preventing subacromial impingement.

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In therapeutic electrotherapy, what is the clinical distinction between 'Acupuncture-Like TENS' (Low-Frequency TENS: 2–5 Hz) and 'Conventional TENS' (High-Frequency TENS: 80–120 Hz)?
options: Acupuncture-like TENS uses radio waves that destroy subcutaneous nociceptor endings
There is zero physiological or clinical difference between high and low-frequency TENS
Conventional TENS stimulates bone mineral growth through direct galvanic direct current
It uses low frequency and stronger intensity to promote endogenous opioid analgesia
explanation: Acupuncture-like TENS (2–5 Hz, high intensity producing visible muscle twitches) stimulates A-delta/C fibers to activate the descending periaqueductal gray-endorphinergic system, producing systemic opioid analgesia with delayed onset but longer duration.

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In therapeutic ultrasound, why is a frequency of '3 MHz' selected over '1 MHz' when treating superficial tendons (e.g., Lateral Epicondyle, Patellar Tendon)?
options: 1 MHz ultrasound is completely blocked by the epidermis and cannot enter biological tissue
3 MHz ultrasound penetrates through the entire human body to a depth of 20 centimeters
Higher-frequency ultrasound is absorbed more superficially, whereas lower frequency penetrates deeper
3 MHz ultrasound produces high-voltage electrical shocks that stimulate muscle contraction
explanation: Acoustic absorption increases with frequency. 3 MHz ultrasound energy is absorbed superficially (depth ~1–2.5 cm, ideal for epicondyles/patellar tendon), while 1 MHz penetrates deeply (depth ~3–5 cm, ideal for deep hip/spine).

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: In therapeutic laser therapy (Low-Level Laser Therapy / Photobiomodulation - PBM), what is the primary intracellular photoreceptor (chromophore) that absorbs red and near-infrared light?
options: Nuclear DNA double-helix strands located inside osteoclast bone cells
Melanin pigments located exclusively in the stratum corneum of the epidermis
Hemoglobin iron molecules inside circulating red blood cell erythrocytes exclusively
Cytochrome c oxidase is the mitochondrial chromophore for red and near-infrared light
explanation: Photobiomodulation (600–1000 nm) targets Cytochrome c Oxidase (Unit IV of the mitochondrial respiratory chain), stimulating electron transport, increasing ATP synthesis, modulating ROS signaling, and promoting cellular repair.

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In cryotherapy, what is the 'Hunting Reaction' (Lewis Reaction)?
options: Sudden permanent necrosis of deep muscle tissue caused by 2 minutes of ice application
A massive spike in core body temperature up to 42 degrees Celsius during cold immersion
Spontaneous involuntary twitching of the facial cranial nerves during winter sports
It is alternating cold-induced vasoconstriction and vasodilation during prolonged cooling
explanation: The Hunting reaction (Lewis) describes transient cold-induced vasodilation (CIVD) alternating with vasoconstriction during prolonged tissue cooling, thought to represent a local protective mechanism against ischemic tissue damage.

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In iontophoresis, what is the chemical polarity and electrode placement rule for driving 'Dexamethasone Sodium Phosphate' (a negatively charged anti-inflammatory corticosteroid) transdermally?
options: Placed under the anode, the positive electrode, because opposite charges repel
Placed equally under both electrodes using high-frequency alternating current units
Dexamethasone phosphate is placed under the cathode because like charges repel
Iontophoresis cannot be used with pharmacological agents under any clinical conditions
explanation: In iontophoresis, like charges repel: negatively charged dexamethasone ions are placed under the negative active electrode (Cathode) to drive them electrostatically into the underlying inflamed tissue.

subtopic: Neuro-rehabilitation concepts and motor relearning
text: In neurological rehabilitation, what is the 'Motor Relearning Programme' (Carr & Shepherd)?
options: An electrotherapy protocol applying continuous galvanic current to the skull
A passive therapy relying strictly on full-body warm whirlpool immersion baths
It uses task-oriented practice guided by movement analysis and functional goals
A system of rigid full-leg splints used to immobilize stroke patients in bed for 12 months
explanation: Carr and Shepherd's Motor Relearning Programme (MRP) is a cognitive, task-oriented behavioral approach focusing on analyzing essential movement components, retraining motor control in real functional contexts, and preventing learned compensations.

subtopic: Neuro-rehabilitation concepts and motor relearning
text: In Rood's Approach to neuro-facilitation, which cutaneous sensory stimulation techniques are categorized as 'Facilitatory' to activate a flaccid muscle?
options: Total darkness and complete sensory deprivation in a quiet room
Rood facilitation uses fast brushing, quick stroking, icing, and muscle tapping
Continuous passive immobilization in a fiberglass cast without tactile stimulation
Slow rhythmic rocking, neutral warmth, sustained deep tendon pressure, and slow stroking
explanation: Rood's facilitatory techniques (fast brushing, quick icing, light stroking, muscle tapping) activate high-threshold cutaneous and muscle spindle afferents to increase motoneuron pool excitability in flaccid muscles.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In the assessment of Spasticity, what is the 'Modified Ashworth Scale' (MAS) Grade '1+' defined as?
options: Complete flaccidity with zero resistance to passive movement in the joint
Considerable increase in tone, passive movement difficult throughout the entire range
This grade shows a catch followed by slight resistance through part of the range
Affected parts are rigid in flexion or extension with no passive movement
explanation: MAS Grade 1+: Slight increase in muscle tone, manifested by a catch followed by minimal resistance through less than half of the remaining range of motion. (Grade 1 has catch/release at end of range; Grade 2 has resistance through most of range).

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: In Vestibular Rehabilitation, what is the 'Epley Maneuver' (Canalith Repositioning Procedure) specifically designed to treat?
options: Cervical facet joint arthrosis producing mechanical neck stiffness during rotation
The Epley maneuver treats posterior-canal BPPV by moving otoconia into the utricle
Acoustic neuroma compression of the vestibulocochlear cranial nerve in the brainstem
Meniere's disease caused by chronic endolymphatic hydrops throughout the cochlea
explanation: The Epley maneuver utilizes sequential head rotations in the plane of the posterior semicircular canal to guide displaced calcium carbonate otoconia crystals under gravity from the canal lumen back into the utricle.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: In traumatic brain injury rehabilitation, what does Level IV on the 'Rancho Los Amigos Scale of Cognitive Functioning' signify?
options: Confused-Appropriate: Patient shows goal-directed behavior with structured cues
No Response: Patient appears to be in a deep coma and does not respond to any stimuli
Rancho Level IV is confused-agitated behavior with purposeless activity and poor cooperation
Purposeful-Appropriate: Patient is fully alert, oriented, and able to learn new tasks
explanation: Rancho Level IV is the Confused-Agitated stage: the patient is hyperactive, aggressive, disoriented, and reacts bizarrely to environmental stimuli, requiring a structured, low-stimulation management approach.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: When performing Upper Limb Neurodynamic Testing for the Ulnar Nerve (ULTT 3 / Ulnar Nerve Bias), what is the standardized test sequence?
options: Shoulder elevation, internal rotation, elbow full extension, forearm supination, and wrist flexion
Shoulder abduction to 180° with elbow locked in straight extension and thumb flexion
Ulnar nerve testing combines shoulder depression, forearm pronation, wrist extension, and elbow flexion
Shoulder adduction across chest with forearm pronation and elbow locked at 0°
explanation: ULTT 3 (Ulnar nerve bias) sequence: Shoulder depression -> Shoulder abduction (~90°) and external rotation -> Wrist and finger extension -> Forearm pronation -> Full elbow flexion (placing the hand by the ear) -> Contralateral cervical side-bending.

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In Butler's neurodynamics, what is the clinical distinction between a neurodynamic 'Slider' technique and a neurodynamic 'Tensioner' technique?
options: Tensioners completely transect the peripheral nerve sheath to relieve pressure
Sliders are passive heat packs applied over the dermatomal sensory distribution
Sliders are high-velocity manipulations that fracture osteophytes around the nerve root
A slider tensions one end while releasing the other; a tensioner tensions both ends
explanation: Sliders produce longitudinal sliding/flossing of the nerve relative to adjacent tissues with minimal strain (ideal for acute/irritable neural pain). Tensioners pull from both ends simultaneously, restoring viscoelastic tensile capacity in chronic non-irritable conditions.

subtopic: Therapeutic exercise protocols and manual therapy
text: In Maitland manual therapy, what physiological effects are produced by Grade I and II joint oscillations that make them effective for acute painful joints?
options: Permanent structural elongation of thick capsular collagen adhesions
Chemical destruction of substance P receptors inside the synovial membrane
They stimulate mechanoreceptors, reduce pain input, and circulate joint fluid
Immediate bony fusion of the articular joint facets to prevent all motion
explanation: Grade I/II gentle oscillations fire low-threshold mechanoreceptors (Ruffini/Pacinian-like corpuscles) in the joint capsule, closing the pain gate in the dorsal horn (melzack-wall) and improving synovial nutrition without stressing healing tissues.

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Joint biomechanics, muscle levers and force couples
text: In Cyriax's manual medicine, what defines a 'Capsular Pattern' of joint restriction?
options: A structural bone deformity caused by congenital epiphyseal plate dysgenesis
A painless hypermobility where joint range of motion exceeds 300% of normal
An isolated limitation of only one single movement caused by a focal muscle strain
It is a predictable proportional restriction of joint motion caused by capsular involvement
explanation: Cyriax defined the Capsular Pattern as a characteristic, proportional pattern of ROM restriction unique to each joint that occurs when the entire joint capsule is inflamed or contracted (e.g., Shoulder: External Rotation > Abduction > Internal Rotation).

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: What is the Capsular Pattern of the Hip Joint according to Cyriax and Magee?
options: Limitation of Extension only with full Flexion and Abduction
Marked limitation of External Rotation with full, unrestricted Internal Rotation
Equal 100% limitation across all physiological hip movements identically
The hip capsular pattern most limits internal rotation and flexion, then abduction
explanation: The capsular pattern of the hip joint exhibits greatest loss of Internal Rotation and Flexion, followed by Abduction, with relative preservation of External Rotation and Adduction.

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In Mulligan's concept for treating tennis elbow (lateral epicondylalgia), what Mobilization with Movement (MWM) technique is applied at the elbow?
options: Mulligan uses a lateral glide during painless gripping or resisted wrist extension
Passive immobilization of the elbow in 90° of flexion using a fiberglass splint
Continuous axial compression pushing the radius into the capitellum
High-velocity manipulation into forced sudden hyperextension of the elbow joint
explanation: Mulligan's lateral elbow MWM: the therapist applies a sustained lateral glide to the forearm bones while stabilizing the humerus, and the patient performs the previously painful movement (e.g., gripping or wrist extension), yielding immediate pain-free force generation.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In lumbar spine biomechanics, what is the 'Neutral Zone' described by Manohar Panjabi?
options: The space between the L5 vertebra and the sacral promontory where nerves emerge
The point of maximum structural failure where spinal ligaments rupture completely
It is low-resistance motion around neutral posture controlled by local stabilizing muscles
The area of the spinal cord where primary motor neurons decussate in the medulla
explanation: Panjabi's Neutral Zone (NZ) is the zone of high joint laxity around neutral alignment where spinal motion encounters low passive resistance. Injury/degeneration enlarges the NZ (instability), requiring local active muscular stabilization (multifidus/TrA) to control it.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: During cervical vascular-risk assessment, which finding should stop treatment and prompt appropriate referral?
options: Complete disappearance of all deep tendon reflexes in the lower limbs
Neurovascular warning symptoms during neck movement require referral
Localized muscular soreness in the upper trapezius muscle belly
Audible clicking of the temporomandibular joint during jaw opening
explanation: Dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, drop attacks, nausea, numbness, or nystagmus during or after a neck movement are concerning symptoms. Modern frameworks do not treat sustained extension–rotation testing as a valid stand-alone vascular screen; history, examination, risk assessment, and referral are required.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'McMurray Test' is performed to detect meniscal tears in the knee. What maneuver specifically tests the Posterior Horn of the Medial Meniscus?
options: Fully flexing the knee, applying Internal Tibial Rotation and Varus Stress, and extending the knee
External rotation and valgus during extension stress the posteromedial meniscus.
Applying downward axial compression on the patella in full knee hyperextension
Applying pure anterior translation of the proximal tibia in 20° of knee flexion
explanation: In McMurray's test, external tibial rotation with valgus stress brings the posterior horn of the medial meniscus between the femoral condyle and tibial plateau; a palpable click or pain during extension is diagnostic.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Apley's Grind Test' (Compression Test) vs 'Apley's Distraction Test' in the prone position with the knee at 90° flexion differentiates:
options: Deep vein thrombosis from gastrocnemius muscle belly strain
Compression tests menisci; distraction tests collateral ligaments.
Anterior cruciate ligament tear from posterior cruciate ligament rupture
Patellar tendinitis from quadriceps tendon rupture
explanation: Apley's maneuver: Axial downward compression + rotation compresses the menisci (pain = meniscal tear). Axial upward distraction + rotation offloads menisci while stressing collateral ligaments/capsule (pain = ligamentous sprain).

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Jobe Relocation Test' (Modified Fowler Sign) is performed immediately following a positive Anterior Apprehension test of the shoulder by:
options: Placing an ice pack directly over the clavicle while the patient stands upright
Forcefully pulling the arm into pure adduction and internal rotation across the chest
Applying high-velocity axial distraction to dislocate the humeral head inferiorly
Posterior pressure on the humeral head reduces apprehension and permits external rotation.
explanation: The Jobe Relocation test applies a posterior force to the anterior proximal humerus, preventing anterior subluxation; immediate relief of apprehension and increased pain-free external rotation confirms anterior capsulolabral instability.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Cozen's Test' and 'Mill's Test' are clinical orthopedic tests used to diagnose:
options: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (Median nerve compression at the flexor retinaculum)
Cozen and Mill tests assess lateral epicondylalgia involving the wrist extensor origin.
Cubital Tunnel Syndrome (Ulnar nerve compression at the medial epicondyle)
Medial Epicondylalgia (Golfer's Elbow - Flexor Carpi Radialis pathology)
explanation: Cozen's test (resisted wrist extension with radial deviation and pronation) and Mill's test (passive wrist flexion, forearm pronation, and elbow extension) stress the ECRB tendon origin at the lateral epicondyle.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Thomas Test' is performed to assess hip flexor contracture. If the extended thigh remains elevated off the examination table while the knee flexes to 90°, and extending the knee allows the thigh to drop flat to the table, the tightness is localized to:
options: Pectineus and Adductor Brevis medial muscles
Iliopsoas muscle belly, the one-joint primary hip flexor
Tensor Fasciae Latae / Iliotibial Band complex
Rectus femoris, a two-joint hip flexor and knee extensor.
explanation: In the modified Thomas test, if the thigh touches the table when the knee is extended (slackening the rectus femoris across the knee) but elevates when the knee is flexed to 90°, isolated Rectus Femoris contracture is confirmed.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Ober's Test' evaluates contracture or tightness of which lower extremity soft-tissue structure?
options: Gastrocnemius and Soleus deep calf compartment musculature
The iliotibial band and tensor fasciae latae.
Iliopsoas muscle complex inside the retroperitoneal space
Hamstring muscle group, semitendinosus and semimembranosus
explanation: Ober's test (patient side-lying, examiner abducts and extends the tested hip with knee flexed to 90°, then allows the thigh to drop into adduction): failure of the knee to adduct past the table midline indicates ITB/TFL contracture.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Thompson Test' (Simmonds' Squeeze Test) is diagnostic for complete rupture of the Achilles tendon when:
options: Squeezing the calf elicits normal brisk ankle plantarflexion of 20°
Squeezing the calf causes immediate severe ankle dorsiflexion
The patient can perform 50 single-leg calf raises without any pain
Absent passive plantarflexion after calf squeeze indicates Achilles rupture.
explanation: Thompson/Simmonds test: with patient prone and feet hanging off the table, squeezing the calf normally produces passive plantarflexion. Absence of foot movement confirms complete rupture of the Achilles tendon.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'FADIR Test' (Flexion, Adduction, Internal Rotation) of the hip is the primary physical assessment screening test for:
options: Sacroiliac joint anterior ligamentous sprain
Hamstring avulsion fracture from the ischial tuberosity
Trochanteric bursitis over the lateral greater trochanter
FADIR screens for femoroacetabular impingement and labral injury.
explanation: The FADIR test flexes the hip to 90°, adducts, and internally rotates, jamming the femoral head-neck junction against the anterosuperior acetabular rim. Groin pain reproduction is highly sensitive (>95%) for FAI and labral tears.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In the daily adjustable progressive resistance exercise (DAPRE) system (Kenneth Knight), how is the resistance for Set 4 and the next training session determined?
options: DAPRE adjusts resistance from completed repetitions using an objective chart.
By asking the patient to guess how much weight they would like to lift
By arbitrarily doubling the weight every single day regardless of performance
By decreasing the resistance by 50% after every single completed set
explanation: Knight's DAPRE protocol utilizes a 4-set system with an objective autoregulation table: the number of repetitions achieved in Set 3 (at 100% estimated 6RM) dictates the exact load for Set 4 and the starting working weight for the next session.

subtopic: Therapeutic exercise protocols and manual therapy
text: In the rehabilitation of hamstring strains, what is the 'Nordic Hamstring Exercise' (NHE) and what is its primary biomechanical stimulus?
options: A seated leg curl performed with rapid concentric contractions on an isokinetic dynamometer
A passive hamstring stretch held for 10 minutes continuously while seated on the floor
Nordics are partner-assisted kneeling lowers that load the hamstrings eccentrically at long lengths.
A standing high-knee marching drill performed with zero external resistance
explanation: The Nordic Hamstring Exercise produces supramaximal eccentric torque as the hamstrings resist forward torso fall, stimulating sarcomerogenesis (fascicle lengthening) and reducing hamstring strain injury incidence by up to 51%.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In manual therapy according to Maitland, what defines a 'Grade III' joint mobilization technique?
options: Grade III uses large oscillations into resistance up to the available range limit.
A small-amplitude oscillation performed within the pain-free starting range of movement
A gentle vibration technique held for 5 seconds to reduce skin temperature
A high-velocity thrust manipulation performed under general hospital anesthesia
explanation: Maitland Grade III is a large-amplitude oscillation moving from mid-range deep into tissue resistance (stretching the joint capsule and periarticular adhesions), used to treat joint stiffness dominant conditions.

subtopic: Therapeutic exercise protocols and manual therapy
text: In PNF stretching, what is the neurophysiological mechanism underlying 'Agonist Contraction' (AC) stretching?
options: Agonist contraction uses reciprocal inhibition to relax the opposing tight muscle.
Autogenic inhibition mediated by Golgi tendon organs in the non-contracting limb
Direct sympathetic vasoconstriction shutting down arterial blood flow to the muscle
Complete destruction of all alpha motor neuron cell bodies in the ventral horn
explanation: Agonist Contraction utilizes reciprocal inhibition (Sherrington): contracting the agonist muscle (e.g., quadriceps) fires Ia afferents that excite Ia inhibitory interneurons, inhibiting alpha motoneurons of the antagonist (hamstrings) to facilitate stretch.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: In shoulder rehabilitation, what are the 'Blackburn Exercises' designed to recruit and strengthen?
options: Heavy overhead barbell bench press exercises targeting the anterior deltoid
They strengthen the posterior rotator cuff and lower and middle trapezius.
Standing bicep curls performed with heavy dumbbells to muscular failure
Seated internal rotation exercises targeting the subscapularis exclusively
explanation: Blackburn exercises (prone T, Y, W, L positions with thumb pointing up) systematically activate the lower trapezius, middle trapezius, infraspinatus, and supraspinatus with high EMG-to-upper trapezius ratios.

subtopic: Therapeutic exercise protocols and manual therapy
text: In the McKenzie Method (MDT), what characterizes the 'Dysfunction Syndrome' of spinal pain?
options: Pain caused by an acute herniated disc that centralizes immediately with 10 repetitions
It is end-range pain from shortened or scarred tissue without rapid range change.
Pain produced only when the athlete is sleeping in a completely neutral posture
Constant unremitting pain that radiates down into both legs during bed rest
explanation: Dysfunction Syndrome in MDT results from structural contracture/adhesion of periarticular tissue: pain is felt consistently at end-range (not in mid-range), does not centralize rapidly, and requires progressive remodeling stretching over weeks.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In kinesiology, what is the 'Convex-Concave Rule' for the Talocrural Joint during active open-chain ankle Dorsiflexion?
options: The convex talus rolls anteriorly and glides anteriorly in the exact same direction
The concave mortise rolls posteriorly and glides anteriorly on the fixed talar dome
The talus undergoes pure superior vertical elevation without any anterior-posterior roll
In dorsiflexion, the convex talus rolls anteriorly and glides posteriorly.
explanation: In open-chain ankle dorsiflexion, the convex trochlea of the talus moves within the concave mortise. By Kaltenborn's convex-concave rule, the talus rolls anteriorly and slides posteriorly.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In human gait, what is the 'Third Ankle Rocker' (Forefoot Rocker / Toe Rocker) during the Pre-Swing / Push-Off phase?
options: The heel strikes the ground and decelerates forward tibial momentum
The body rolls over the metatarsophalangeal joints as the calf produces push-off.
The foot remains completely flat on the floor while the knee hyperextends
The entire lower limb swings in the air without any contact with the ground
explanation: The 3rd rocker (forefoot/toe rocker) occurs from heel-off to toe-off: the MTP joints act as a fulcrum, the plantar fascia tightens via windlass mechanism, and calf recoil propels the limb into swing.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In patellofemoral biomechanics, what is the 'Q-Angle' (Quadriceps Angle), and what are the standard normal values in adult males and females?
options: It links ASIS, patella, and tibial tuberosity, usually larger in females.
The ankle angle in maximum dorsiflexion, normal at 90 degrees
The angle of thoracic ribcage rotation during maximum deep inhalation
The angle between the femur and vertical, normal at 45 degrees in both sexes
explanation: The Q-angle quantifies the lateral pull vector of the quadriceps on the patella. Normal values are 10°–14° for males and 15°–18° for females (due to wider pelvis); values >20° increase lateral patellar subluxation risk.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: An 'Antalgic Gait' is characterized by:
options: Rhythmic lateral trunk lurching over the stance hip due to gluteus medius paralysis
Antalgic gait shortens stance on the painful limb to reduce weight-bearing and pain.
Hyper-extension of the bilateral knees during the terminal swing flight phase
Excessive hip and knee flexion to clear a paralyzed dropping foot from the floor
explanation: Antalgic gait is a pain-avoidance adaptation: the athlete shortens the stance time on the injured extremity to unload the painful structure as quickly as possible, producing an asymmetrical, abbreviated step cadence.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In hip biomechanics, what is the clinical consequence of an excessive 'Femoral Anteversion' angle (>20°–25°)?
options: Complete structural dislocation of the femoral head out of the obturator foramen
Loss of all sagittal hip flexion range of motion during athletic sprinting
Excess anteversion increases internal rotation, reduces external rotation, and promotes in-toeing.
Marked limitation of internal rotation with excessive external rotation and out-toeing gait
explanation: Normal femoral anteversion is 8°–15°. Excessive anteversion (>20°–25°) directs the femoral head anteriorly; the athlete compensates by internally rotating the limb to seat the head in the acetabulum, producing in-toeing and higher valgus strain.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: In scapular kinematics, what is 'Scapular Dyskinesis' and how is Type I Dyskinesis (Kibler Classification) clinically identified?
options: Prominence of the entire medial scapular border during movement
Superior migration of the entire scapula with excessive upper trapezius dominance
Type I dyskinesis shows inferior-angle prominence from anterior scapular tipping.
Symmetrical scapular movement without any structural or kinematic abnormalities
explanation: Kibler's classification: Type I = Inferior medial border prominence (inferior angle tipping, lower trap weakness); Type II = Entire medial border prominence (winging, serratus weakness); Type III = Superior border prominence.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: During the 'Initial Swing' (Acceleration) phase of normal walking gait, which muscle group contracts concentrically to advance the trailing limb forward?
options: Quadriceps femoris contracting eccentrically to lock the knee in hyperextension
Hip extensors and hamstrings of the posterior kinetic chain
Gastrocnemius and soleus contracting isometrically to anchor the heel
Hip flexors and pretibial dorsiflexors advance the limb during initial swing.
explanation: Initial Swing begins when the foot leaves the ground: the iliopsoas/rectus femoris contract concentrically to accelerate the thigh forward, while the tibialis anterior dorsiflexes the ankle to ensure ground clearance.

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In kinesiology, what is 'Active Insufficiency' of a multi-joint muscle?
options: It is reduced force when a multi-joint muscle is maximally shortened across its joints.
The inability of a muscle to lengthen fully across all joints due to passive tension
A permanent structural severance of the motor nerve axon leading to flaccid paralysis
Complete energetic depletion of ATP in the sarcoplasmic reticulum during every contraction
explanation: Active insufficiency occurs when a multi-joint muscle is shortened across all of its joints and cannot generate maximal active tension. For example, the hamstrings may generate less knee-flexion force when the hip is extended and the knee is already flexed.

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Joint biomechanics, muscle levers and force couples
text: In therapeutic electrotherapy, what is the 'Accommodation' phenomenon in peripheral nerve fibers during electrical stimulation?
options: The complete destruction of the nerve myelin sheath by high-frequency radio waves
The conversion of motor nerves into sensory receptor cells under direct current
Accommodation raises the depolarization threshold during a slowly rising electrical current.
The rapid growth of new collateral nerve axons within 5 minutes of stimulation
explanation: Accommodation: if an electrical stimulus rises slowly, the resting membrane potential adapts (inactivation of voltage-gated Na+ channels and opening of K+ channels), increasing the threshold required to initiate an action potential.

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In therapeutic ultrasound, what is 'Acoustic Microstreaming' and 'Stable Cavitation'?
options: Rapid thermal boiling and vaporization of synovial fluid inside the joint cavity
Direct electrical depolarization of sensory nociceptor nerve endings
Violent implosion and collapse of gas bubbles causing extensive tissue necrosis
They create nonthermal fluid motion that can influence membrane permeability.
explanation: Stable cavitation (rhythmic oscillation of gas bubbles without collapse) and acoustic microstreaming (unidirectional fluid currents) are non-thermal ultrasound mechanisms that alter cellular membrane permeability, upregulating fibroblast repair.

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In shortwave diathermy, what is the clinical distinction between 'Inductive Coil' (Magnetic Field) applicators and 'Capacitive Plate' (Electric Field) applicators?
options: There is zero physical or thermal difference between inductive and capacitive diathermy
Capacitive plates penetrate 10 times deeper than inductive coils in all human tissues
Inductive coils produce ionizing radiation that fractures bone trabeculae
Inductive coils heat conductive deep tissue, while capacitive plates heat superficial tissue.
explanation: Inductive diathermy generates magnetic fields that induce circular eddy currents in high-conductivity tissues (muscle/vascular beds), heating deep muscle without overheating subcutaneous fat (which occurs under capacitive electric fields).

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In cryotherapy, what is the primary clinical advantage of 'Cryokinetics' (combining cold application with active exercise) in acute sports injury rehabilitation?
options: Cryokinetics uses cold analgesia to permit early pain-free functional exercise.
Cold completely freezes the joint capsule in a rigid, immobile close-packed position
Cryokinetics is strictly contraindicated in all musculoskeletal sports conditions
Active exercise during icing permanently destroys all nociceptive sensory nerve endings
explanation: Cryokinetics (Knight): applying ice until numbness is achieved allows the athlete to initiate early, pain-free active range of motion and functional exercises, preventing arthrogenic inhibition, muscle atrophy, and joint stiffness.

subtopic: Observational and pathological gait analysis
text: In neuromuscular electrical stimulation, what is the 'Order of Motor Unit Recruitment' under electrical stimulation compared to normal physiological voluntary contraction?
options: Electrical stimulation never recruits any motor units under any frequency parameters
Electrical stimulation recruits small Type I slow-twitch units first, identical to voluntary recruitment
Electrical stimulation often recruits large fast units first, unlike voluntary recruitment.
Electrical stimulation recruits smooth involuntary muscle fibers exclusively
explanation: In NMES, large-diameter axons (innervating Type II fibers) have lower internal electrical resistance to externally applied current, causing them to depolarize first—reversing Henneman's normal size principle and causing rapid fatigue.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: In neuro-rehabilitation, what is the 'Task-Specific Training' approach (Locomotor Training / Body-Weight-Supported Treadmill Training - BWSTT)?
options: Applying passive heat packs to the lumbar spine for 60 minutes without active stepping
Relying exclusively on seated leg-extension training without practicing walking
Immobilizing the lower extremities in plaster casts while the patient performs arm cycling
It repeats intensive, task-specific walking with harness support to promote neuroplasticity.
explanation: BWSTT uses partial unweighting to allow intensive, repetitive, task-specific stepping, providing sensory afferent cues (hip extension/load) that stimulate spinal Central Pattern Generators (CPGs) and supraspinal neuroplasticity.

subtopic: Therapeutic exercise protocols and manual therapy
text: In Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF), the 'D1 Flexion' pattern of the Upper Extremity consists of which combined triplanar movements?
options: It combines shoulder flexion, adduction, external rotation, and forearm supination.
Shoulder flexion, abduction, and external rotation with forearm supination, a waiter-tray pattern
Shoulder Extension, Adduction, and Internal Rotation with wrist Extension
Shoulder Extension, Abduction, and Internal Rotation with forearm Pronation
explanation: PNF UE D1 Flexion (picking up an apple and putting it in the mouth): Shoulder Flexion + Adduction + External Rotation, Forearm Supination, Wrist/Finger Flexion toward the contralateral ear.

subtopic: Neuro-rehabilitation concepts and motor relearning
text: In stroke rehabilitation, what is the 'Pusher Syndrome' (Contraversive Pushing)?
options: An involuntary tremor of the upper extremity elicited during goal-directed finger pointing
A condition where the patient refuses to walk due to visual blindness
Pusher syndrome involves pushing toward the paretic side and resisting correction to midline.
A sudden loss of all sensation in the bilateral feet caused by peripheral neuropathy
explanation: Pusher Syndrome (Karnath): damage to the posterolateral thalamus alters perceived body verticality (~18° tilted toward the lesion side), leading patients to actively push away from the sound side toward the paralyzed side.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: In sensory ataxia and balance rehabilitation, what constitutes the 'Romberg Test' and what signifies a positive test?
options: Romberg is positive when closing the eyes causes marked sway or loss of balance.
The patient demonstrates high-amplitude resting tremor of the hands in sitting
The patient cannot hear a tuning fork held near the external auditory canal
The patient falls immediately with eyes open, indicating a pure cerebellar vermis lesion
explanation: Romberg's sign: patient stands with feet together; stability with eyes open followed by loss of balance upon eye closure confirms intact cerebellar function but loss of dorsal column somatosensory/proprioceptive input.

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In Parkinson's disease neurorehabilitation, what is the 'LSVT BIG' protocol?
options: A low-intensity bed rest protocol designed to reduce resting metabolic energy expenditure
A pharmaceutical protocol involving continuous intravenous high-dose steroid infusions
LSVT BIG is intensive amplitude-focused exercise for large movements in Parkinson's disease.
A surgical brain ablation procedure performed to destroy the substantia nigra
explanation: LSVT BIG is an intensive (4 days/week for 4 weeks) amplitude-based behavioral training program that uses high physical effort and maximal amplitude movements to recalibrate motor output and overcome hypokinesia.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: During upper-limb neurodynamic testing for a brachial-plexus or peripheral-nerve presentation, which movement can serve as structural differentiation when symptoms are reproduced?
options: Contralateral neck side-bending increases neural symptoms.
Applying ice to the contralateral quadriceps muscle belly
Deep inspiration held for 60 continuous seconds
Passive plantarflexion of the ipsilateral great toe
explanation: Contralateral cervical lateral flexion can increase neural-tissue loading and ipsilateral flexion can reduce it, but the finding must be interpreted with the complete neurodynamic examination; it does not by itself confirm a nerve-root diagnosis.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: In Butler's clinical neurodynamics, what is the anatomical site of the 'Tarsal Tunnel' where the Posterior Tibial Nerve can become entrapped in athletes?
options: Along the dorsum of the foot over the intermediate cuneiform bone
Inside the popliteal fossa between the two heads of the gastrocnemius
It lies behind the medial malleolus beneath the flexor retinaculum.
Beneath the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament on the anterolateral ankle
explanation: The tarsal tunnel lies posteroinferior to the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum, containing the Tibialis posterior, Flexor digitorum longus, Posterior tibial artery/veins, Tibial nerve, and Flexor hallucis longus ('Tom, Dick, ANd Harry').

subtopic: Evidence-based electrophysical modalities
text: In Kaltenborn manual therapy, what is the 'Traction Grade III' (Stretch Traction)?
options: A very small amplitude traction that relieves compressive joint forces without separating surfaces
A traction force applied exclusively to fracture osteophyte bone spurs
A traction force that completely dislocates the joint permanently out of its anatomical socket
Grade III traction takes up slack and stretches the capsule to increase joint mobility.
explanation: Kaltenborn Traction: Grade I = Nullifies joint compressive forces (piccolo); Grade II = Takes up capsule slack ('tightens the joint'); Grade III = Stretches capsular and ligamentous tissue to increase joint play.

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Joint biomechanics, muscle levers and force couples
text: In Cyriax's manual medicine, what constitutes a 'Non-Capsular Pattern' of joint restriction, and what does it typically indicate?
options: A complete loss of all joint range of motion caused by total joint fibrous ankylosis
A proportional limitation of all joint movements indicating diffuse rheumatoid arthritis
It limits selected directions outside the capsular pattern, suggesting a focal lesion.
A painless hypermobility where range of motion is double normal physiological limits
explanation: A non-capsular pattern (limitation in one or two isolated directions only) indicates a localized lesion: internal derangement (loose body/meniscal tear), extra-articular lesion (isolated muscle strain/bursitis), or localized capsular adhesion.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: What is the Close-Packed Position of the Radiocarpal (Wrist) Joint where articular stability is maximal?
options: Neutral 0° position with forearm held in full pronation
The wrist is close-packed in full extension with radial deviation.
Full active Wrist Flexion with maximal Ulnar Deviation
90° of elbow flexion with the fingers tightly clenched in a fist
explanation: The close-packed position of the radiocarpal wrist joint is full extension with slight radial deviation, where carpal bones are tightly compressed against the distal radius and radioulnar articular disc.

subtopic: Therapeutic exercise protocols and manual therapy
text: In Mulligan's concept for treating acute painful cervical rotation, what Natural Apophyseal Glide (NAG) / Sustained Natural Apophyseal Glide (SNAG) technique is applied?
options: Passive immobilization of the neck in a rigid cervical collar for 6 consecutive months
Continuous axial compression pushing the cervical vertebrae directly down into the thoracic spine
A forceful high-velocity thrust manipulation into extreme hyperextension and side-bending
SNAG uses a sustained facet glide while the patient actively rotates pain-free.
explanation: Mulligan Cervical SNAG: the therapist applies a sustained thumb glide along the 45° facet incline plane of the involved cervical vertebra while the patient performs active, pain-free rotation, restoring movement instantly (PILL rule).

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: In core stability assessment, what is the 'Prone Instability Test' (PIT) of the lumbar spine?
options: The test reduces pain when the patient lifts the legs during lumbar pressure.
Applying ice to the lumbar spine to check for thermal sensory paresthesia
The patient stands on one leg and jumps 3 meters into the air
The patient performs 100 continuous sit-ups on a decline bench without resting
explanation: Prone Instability Test (Hicks): PA pressure on the lumbar spine elicits pain with legs on floor. When the patient lifts legs (activating deep paraspinal/gluteal stabilizers), muscular contraction stabilizes the segment and abolishes pain, predicting success with stabilization exercises.

topic: human anatomy joint muscle ligament and nerve
subtopic: Joint biomechanics, muscle levers and force couples
text: In thoracic spine physical therapy, what is 'Thoracic Outlet Syndrome' (TOS) and which three anatomical spaces can cause neurovascular compression of the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels?
options: 1. Femoral triangle, 2. Popliteal fossa, and 3. Tarsal tunnel in the lower limb
1. Suboccipital triangle, 2. Mastoid notch, and 3. Foramen magnum in the skull
TOS involves compression in the interscalene, costoclavicular, or retropectoralis spaces.
1. Carpal tunnel, 2. Cubital tunnel, and 3. Guyon's canal in the wrist and elbow
explanation: TOS involves compression of the brachial plexus (C5-T1) and/or subclavian vessels across three anatomical entrapment tunnels: the Interscalene triangle, Costoclavicular space, and Subcoracoid/Retropectoralis minor space.

subtopic: Special orthopedic physical assessment tests
text: The 'Anterior Drawer Test' of the Knee is performed with the patient supine, knee flexed to 90°, and foot stabilized on the table. A positive test demonstrating >6mm anterior tibial translation evaluates:
options: Posterior cruciate ligament rupture causing posterior tibial sag
Lateral collateral ligament rupture with lateral opening
It tests ACL laxity, especially the anteromedial bundle.
Patellar tendon complete rupture at the inferior pole
